Part 6 Operation and Evolution ​

This Part develops the definitions of objects into explanations of processes. Operation, feedback, learning, maintenance, load, phase, and systemic selection are not narrative terms that can be used interchangeably. They are conditional mechanisms with distinct inferential premises and enabling conditions. The mechanisms also differ in their counterfactuals and stopping points. Naming a mechanism does not supply sufficient conditions. Only when the premises it depends on, its conditions, minimum evidence, and competing explanations all pass can the mechanism be determined to hold in a case, within the specified scale, time window, and identity criterion.

06Note

Understanding this section

Part Six: Operation and Evolution

‘The system is operating’, ‘the system received feedback’, and ‘the system learned’ sound similar but make different commitments. Part Six separates them into checkable process questions, preventing an impressive name from replacing an entire evidence chain.

This part develops the definitions of objects into process explanations. The definition of an object specifies boundaries, states, relations, interfaces, time, scale, and identity criteria; a process explanation asks how inputs change subsequent states through carriers or channels, what conditions enable the process, and which comparisons rule out other explanations. Clearly defining an object does not mean its process mechanism is established.

Operation, feedback, learning, maintenance, load, phase, and selection are not interchangeable narrative terms. An operation can occur without return; a return that causes change need not form learning across rounds; maintaining identity or function need not be learning; a load gap need not form lasting damage; phase change is not automatically object conversion; and differential outcomes do not automatically constitute repeated selection.

Each conditional mechanism must separately state inferential premises, enabling conditions, a mechanism chain, minimum evidence, counterfactuals/competing explanations, and stopping points. ‘What the definition requires’ and ‘why it happens in reality’ are also separate: method requirements specify how the analysis verifies claims; they do not add a physical cause in the world.

Only when tests of dependencies, conditions, minimum evidence, and competing explanations all pass proportionately may the mechanism be determined to hold in a case, within the specified scale profile, time window, and identity criterion. The identity criterion here is only one item of the object's definition, not the whole definition. Complete items, correct names, or a coherent story do not replace actual evidence. Existing domain research retains its conclusions and scope and is not invalidated by lacking formal status under this framework.

This part also limits extrapolation: effective does not mean improved, persistent does not mean it ought to be maintained, retention through selection does not mean superiority, and feasible repair does not mean authority to implement it. Empirical mechanisms are judged separately from normative evaluation, responsibility, and action permission; with insufficient evidence, retain candidates and specific gaps rather than filling unknowns with proven failure or proven success.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Separate everyday narratives into specific mechanism claims; do not let one name account for the whole process.

  2. 2

    Declare the object's definition and the scope of scale, time window, and identity criterion, then state process variables and channels.

  3. 3

    List this mechanism's own dependencies, enabling conditions, chain, and minimum materials.

  4. 4

    Check the claim using proportionate counterfactuals, competing explanations, and failure conditions.

  5. 5

    Report supported domain conclusions, formal mechanism qualification, candidates, and unknowns separately.

  6. 6

    Stop extrapolation beyond the window, scale, identity, or claim scope; evaluation and action go to separate normative/authorization procedures.

Distinctions to keep clear

Mechanism name

Points to a set of conditions and materials that should be satisfied.

≠

Support for a mechanism in a case

Those conditions have actual grounds for a specific object and scope.

Inferential premises/method requirements

Specify how an argument is assembled and tested.

≠

Empirical cause

A channel of effects in the world, which cannot be generated by a method's name.

A process has effects

It correspondingly affects subsequent states.

≠

Net benefits and normative justification

Also require predetermined tasks, prices to be paid, and normative comparisons.

Teaching construction: the same word ‘improvement’ actually hides three questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe device, behaviors, and conditions are constructed, not an assumption of successful actual experiments; formal establishment of each mechanism still requires its own materials.

A fictional device receives an output-error signal and changes its next control quantity; this indicates only possible one-time feedback. If its parameters reset every round, this cannot establish learning across rounds. Someone else replaces worn parts and thereby preserves a predetermined function; that is a maintenance question. All three may coexist, but return, retained use, and maintenance comparisons must be checked separately; calling everything ‘the system evolved’ does not finish the work.

BoundaryDo not infer overall net benefit, value progress, or operational authority from behavioral change.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe system has operated for years, so learning, maintenance, selection, and coevolution are all declared established.

What it limitsLong-term existence is insufficient to satisfy the distinctive conditions of these different mechanisms.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleA method requirement is satisfied, so it is treated as a new empirical cause of system change.

What it limitsThis confuses methodological responsibilities with object-level causal relations; explain them separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • This introduction is not a replacement summary of the entire part; each subsequent mechanism still requires an independent explanation of its distinctive conditions.
  • No real-world mechanism certification is completed automatically by a definitional name.
  • The same event can involve multiple mechanisms, but citing the same material repeatedly does not create multiple independent pieces of evidence.

Scope and open questions

The part introduction explains how to read conditional mechanisms, using explicit constructions to identify questions rather than forcibly attaching historical mechanisms that have not been fully identified.

  3. 3

Why is a one-time return that changes a state not directly called learning?

Learning additionally requires materials such as updates being retained/used and task comparisons, which one feedback event does not automatically supply.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a mechanism receives bounded support, does that imply it deserves permanent maintenance?

No. Empirical effects are separate from normative choices, costs, protection, and authority.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why must a mechanism be tied to a scale, time window, and identity criterion?

Scale, time, and identity conditions limit the conclusion's scope; outside them, the original support cannot be directly reused.

6.1Describing an Operation ​

In briefExplaining an operation requires more than recording its start and finish. The record must include where things came from, which path they took, where changes occurred, whether another route existed, and which parts were not observed.

An account of an operation needs to set out at least the inputs, a specified carrier or channel, state transitions, outputs, environmental conditions, a time window, and any traces that may be left. If the output returns, also set out the return channel, the receiving position, and the item that changes. For a claim about intertemporal effects, first distinguish three things under §4.5: how history formed the current state, how current carriers transmit it, and whether there is any additional historical increment beyond the current representation. Check the materials on timing and mechanism for each. Of these, only the claim of an additional historical increment requires a comparison between a model that takes history into account and a model in which “the current state is already sufficient.” If the operation crosses scales, also complete a mapping that meets the definition of scale transformation (§3.4) and the epistemic constraint “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer” (§4.8.5). Accounting item by item in this way is not meant to force a complex process into a linear chain. It makes it possible to test each delay, loss, alternative channel, gap in evidence, and limit of extrapolation.

6.1Note

Understanding this section

6.1 Describing an operation

Explaining an operation requires more than recording its start and finish. The record must include where things came from, which path they took, where changes occurred, whether another route existed, and which parts were not observed.

An account of an operation must set out at least inputs, specified carriers or channels, state transitions, outputs, environmental conditions, time windows, and possible traces. Inputs and outputs are distinguished by the selected object boundary; an output is not necessarily an ultimate social outcome. The carrier, the channel's transmission, and the items of the state that change need specific referents; ‘the system processed it’ is insufficient.

‘Any traces that may be left’ does not mean every operation must preserve memory permanently. There may be no persistent trace or only a temporary state; but a claim that a trace supports a subsequent effect must locate its carrier, retention window, and use, rather than treating the existence of a log as the entire mechanism.

If an output returns, separately state the return channel, receiving position, and the item that changes. Clarify whether the returned signal derives from an earlier output or is an independent external input; signal arrival and the subsequent change in an item must also remain separate. A basic account of an operation does not directly establish effective feedback, whose formal mechanism requires comparisons under the conditions in 6.2.

For intertemporal effects, first follow 4.5's three questions: how the past formed the current state; how the current carrier retains, updates, and affects later outcomes; and whether history still supplies an additional conditional increment given the stated current state. The first two do not have a hard requirement for a historical-increment test; only the third requires comparing a history-aware model with a current-state-sufficient model and taking on the corresponding requirements of the historical-increment test.

When crossing scales, additionally complete a mapping that meets the definition of scale transformation (§3.4) and the epistemic constraint “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer” (§4.8.5): source and target objects, tasks, variables, preservation/change/loss, and errors must be compatible. Recording names of two levels cannot replace mapping, nor can a local effect automatically become an effect on the entire organization or population.

Accounting item by item in this way does not force an actual process into a one-way straight line. There may be parallel inputs, branching, loops, common conditions, and alternative paths; specify delays, losses, capacities, or boundaries individually so each can be observed, compared, or retained as unknown. If evidence breaks at a segment, identify the conclusion it limits rather than inferring that all intermediate channels were correct from a normal final output.

Use accounts of an operation together with their windows and extrapolation boundaries. One execution can support what happened in that round, but does not alone establish long-term stability, continuous learning, comprehensive repair, or net benefit. Preserve the missingness types of unobserved periods and missing items; connecting lines in a process diagram must not become proofs unsupported by materials.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Before results, fix the object boundary, task, variables, time window, and environment, and clarify the definitions of inputs and outputs.

  2. 2

    Specify each carrier/channel's start, endpoint, transmitted content, and state-update rule.

  3. 3

    State parallel and alternative paths, delays, losses, and possible traces without forcing a single chain.

  4. 4

    Where return exists, trace it to the original output, receiving position, and the item changed, then compare according to feedback responsibilities.

  5. 5

    For intertemporal claims, select the historical-formation, carrier-transmission, or additional-historical-increment route and list their materials separately.

  6. 6

    For cross-scale claims, add object and variable bridges under scale transformation and “Testing Cross-Scale Transfer”, and retain task-relevant losses.

  7. 7

    Explain checkable facts, breaks in evidence, and extrapolation ceilings segment by segment; do not invent intermediate processes from a normal endpoint.

Distinctions to keep clear

Output

A result under the current object boundary and window.

≠

Long-term ultimate effects

Require separate intertemporal materials and targets and are not guaranteed by one output.

Trace formation

A carrier preserves a record or state.

≠

Subsequent effect

A trace is used and affects the predetermined outcome; evidence is still required.

Return signal

A feedback path from an earlier output/state.

≠

Independent input

May also change the system but is not that return channel.

Account of an operation

Make paths and gaps inspectable.

≠

Linear-chain assumption

Not a requirement of the account of an operation; networks, loops, and parallel channels are permitted.

Mathematical construction: parallel inputs and losses both affect state recordsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn exact nonnegative inventory model with no additional unrecorded flows; all numbers are artificial stipulations, not actual equipment observations.

A fictional container begins with inventory x=5, two input channels u₁=2 and u₂=1, delivered output q=3 this round, and environmental leakage ℓ=1. Stipulate common units and the same window, with inputs arriving first and combined delivery and leakage no greater than the available quantity. The update is x′=x+u₁+u₂−q−ℓ=4. Recording only the first channel incorrectly predicts 3; omitting leakage predicts 5. The endpoint 4 alone cannot tell us which combination of inputs and losses produced it; process materials must be checked.

BoundaryThis establishes only the accounting mapping and identifies neither actual causation nor long-term capacity stability.

Teaching construction: trace a return to its output sourceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe target, comparator, and planning rule are all constructed; only the planning item's rule-governed update is claimed, without assuming execution or future benefits.

Continuing the fictional container, let the predetermined delivery target be r=4. A comparator reads this round's actual q=3, computes e=r−q=1, returns it through the specified channel to the scheduling position, and changes next round's plan for the first channel u₁ from 2 to 3. The record should preserve q, e's source, the receiving position, and the change in the planning item separately. If the plan has not yet been executed, actual delivery in the next round cannot be declared improved; if the signal is merely an independent external notice, it cannot masquerade as a return from q.

BoundaryActual feedback, subsequent delivery, and persistent learning must be judged from their respective materials.

Mathematical construction: a sufficient current carrier needs no additional historyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn exact fixed rule and complete current s; no actual historical-effect detection.

Let state s update by s′=0.5s+u. Histories (4,0) and (0,2), starting from 0, both reach current s=2. With next input 0, both reach 1. Past inputs have affected current s, but given complete s no additional history is needed to calculate the next step. If only ‘whether s>0’ is stored, history may recover lost distinctions; that is a representation choice that must be disclosed.

BoundaryModel sufficiency does not establish the sufficiency of an actual current state; actual carrier and history routes require separate evidence.

STS-114: imagery, analysis, and actual action occupy different positionsDocumented case

NASA's STS-114 mission record describes how imagery during the 2005 flight revealed two protruding gap fillers, after which mission managers studied whether they needed attention; on August 3, Robinson pulled them out during an extravehicular activity. The record separates observation, analysis/decision, and execution; ‘obtaining imagery’ cannot substitute for completion of the action.

Scope and limitsAn institutional mission record supporting this imagery and removal operation; a single operation does not establish that all safety improvements were effective, long-term learning, or a complete formal feedback case.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleFinal delivery is normal, so none of the original channels failed.

What it limitsSubstitute channels may compensate; an endpoint cannot uniquely recover the path.

What it limitsTraces, invocation, task results, and net benefit each require evidence.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not require a historical-increment test for every intertemporal effect or treat failure to pass the historical-increment test as proof of the carrier route.
  • Absence of traces does not automatically cancel a round of operation or transient feedback; claims of persistence require proportionate preservation materials.
  • A normal output can result from compensation through alternative channels and cannot establish that every original path was functioning normally.
  • A process example is not certification of an actual mechanism; action still requires independent authority and protection.

Scope and open questions

Specific task records provide distinct stages from observation to execution, suitable for illustrating the account of an operation; the diagram and inventory example are separate explicit constructions and fabricate no NASA numbers.

  1. 1

    Why is the inventory example 4 rather than 3 or 5?

  2. 2

    Must the account of an operation be drawn as a straight line?

Why is the inventory example 4 rather than 3 or 5?

Both inputs arrive and leakage occurs: 5+2+1−3−1=4; 3 omits the second input, while 5 omits leakage.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If the planning item has changed, may the next round's actual output be recorded as improved?

No. Check whether plans enter execution and actual results occur; an update of this item cannot replace future observation.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Do all intertemporal effects require comparison with a history-aware model?

No. Only a claim of additional historical increment beyond the stated current state requires the corresponding comparison; formation and carrier transmission have separate routes.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Must the account of an operation be drawn as a straight line?

Not necessarily. Parallel, return, branching, and substitute channels may be stated; each segment needs a checkable identity and boundary.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

6.2Effective Feedback (CM-FEEDBACK) ​

In briefReceiving comments, receiving an alarm, or saving a report is not yet effective feedback in this section’s sense. Trace how an earlier output returns and precisely where that return changes the next step.

Grounds: the definition “Effective Feedback” (§3.3); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). These three are method requirements, not additional empirical causes. The “Effective Feedback” mechanism does not presuppose a historical increment (§4.5).

The enabling conditions are as follows. A prior state or output enters a later process through a specified return channel that a channel-effect test has identified. Compared with the case of no return or a blocked channel, at least one subsequent state, transition probability, or constraint differs by more than the threshold. The temporal order and which item is changed have been stated before the results are seen. The mechanism chain is:

Prior state or output → return signal → transmission through the specified channel → signal uptake at the receiving position → change in a subsequent state, probability, or constraint → review against a blocking counterfactual

Minimum evidence includes a channel-effect test that has met its pre-registered criteria; the return channel and receiving position; temporal order; the item that changed; the subsequent difference; and a comparison with the case of no return or a blocked channel. Effective feedback is not determined in any of three cases: the signal arrives but the subsequent transition is unchanged; an independent common input can explain the change; or the difference is unchanged after the return channel is cut. Effective feedback establishes only that the return caused a subsequent change on that occasion. It does not amount to learning, repair, or a positive outcome, and it requires no durable historical trace.

6.2Note

Understanding this section

6.2 Effective Feedback (CM-FEEDBACK)

Receiving comments, receiving an alarm, or saving a report is not yet effective feedback in this section’s sense. Trace how an earlier output returns and precisely where that return changes the next step.

This mechanism expands the definition of effective feedback (§3.3) into empirical responsibilities. The definition says what effective feedback is, and a channel-effect test (§4.4) identifies the specified return channel’s effect; the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) set methods for competing explanations, causal identification, and material review, rather than adding causes of change in the world. Basic feedback requires neither a historical-increment test (§4.5) nor permanently retained history.

Enabling conditions include three indispensable connections. First, the signal must originate in a prior state or output and enter a later process through a named channel. Second, relative to no return or blockage, at least one subsequent state, transition probability, or constraint stated in advance must differ beyond a threshold. Third, timing and the item that changes must be stated before the results are seen, not selected as targets after seeing what changed.

The mechanism chain is prior state/output, return signal, transmission through the specified channel, uptake at the receiver, change in a subsequent state, probability, or constraint, and blocked-counterfactual review. The first five describe the claimed causal path; the last is the comparative responsibility for testing that path, not a physical blockage that must occur after every actual operation. A diagram without material for its segments remains a candidate explanation.

Formal minimum evidence includes a channel-effect test that has met its pre-registered criteria, return channel and receiver, temporal order, the item that changed, subsequent differences, and a proportionate no-return/blockage comparison. Controlled intervention, controlled perturbation, or natural variation with identification conditions must follow the preselected plan; identifying actual feedback does not justify arbitrarily shutting safety channels. Suitable existing material can be analyzed first; experiments separately require authority and risk review.

Three failures occur at different positions: a signal arrives but leaves subsequent transitions unchanged, so reception cannot masquerade as effect; shared external input adequately explains the change, so this return has not been distinguished; differences persist after blocking the specified return, failing to support its claimed contribution. Compensation by substitute channels, an intervention not actually taking effect, and insensitive measurement still require checks; one nonsignificant result does not prove that ‘no feedback of any kind exists’.

Effective means that return has an effect, not that it is good. It may correct deviations or amplify error, delay decisions, or cause losses; one effective return is not automatically learning across rounds, repair, or net benefit. Section 6.2.1 uses a fully specified mathematical model to prove that ‘the same first-step change’ and ‘different long-term stability’ can coexist. Model comparisons do not constitute a real channel-effect test.

Process facts and causal research in domain reports retain their standing under their own material. Absence of this framework’s complete pre-registration of a formal test does not cancel rule changes or actual execution that occurred; equally, those facts cannot retrospectively establish every specified mechanism and long-term effect. Conclusions should explicitly distinguish observed changes, mechanism candidates, and still-unidentified parts.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First state object, window, target items, return origin, and receiver, confirming that the signal is not an independent external input.

  2. 2

    List the inferential responsibilities of the definition of effective feedback and of the channel effect separately from the three methodological responsibilities: “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals,” the conditions for causal claims, and the conditions for evidence; do not add a requirement that basic feedback undergo a historical-increment test.

  3. 3

    Before results, fix the primary comparison, threshold, timing, and measured channel dimensions, and check the execution version.

  4. 4

    Trace transmission, uptake, and subsequent change through material, separating arrival, traces, and effect.

  5. 5

    Use proportionate no-return, blockage, or alternative comparisons with identification conditions, addressing shared inputs, substitute channels, and measurement changes.

  6. 6

    With insufficient evidence, record only candidates and gaps; null conclusions additionally require their rules, sensitivity, and tolerances.

  7. 7

    For a supported effect, separately ask about stability, learning, target improvement, loss distribution, and authority; ‘effective’ cannot answer everything.

Distinctions to keep clear

Signal arrival

The receiver has the signal, which may generate only a receipt.

≠

Effective feedback

The specified return creates an identifiable difference in a predetermined subsequent item.

Return effect

May follow a fixed rule and occur only once.

≠

Learning

Additionally requires retention of updates, actual invocation, task comparison, and other conditions.

No-return counterfactual

A comparison condition helping distinguish this channel’s effect.

≠

Actual forced disconnection required

Not a logical requirement; real tests remain constrained by safety, authority, and feasibility.

Method requirements

Constrains testing and treatment of competing explanations.

≠

Causes in the object

Channels or conditions actually transmitting change.

Mathematical construction: transient feedback exists without permanent memoryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExact deterministic rules, with return as the sole update source and blockage changing no other conditions; entirely a mathematical setup, not a real device experiment.

Each round, a device outputs a=0 with target r=1. A comparator reads actual a and generates e=r−a=1, returning it through a channel to a controller, which updates a←a+e to 1. Blocking return leaves the rule without input, so a remains 0. With a predetermined model criterion of a within-round output difference greater than 0.5, difference 1 passes. Every state resets to zero after each round, the next round repeats, and no parameters, logs, or experience are retained. The construction thus has return effects this round but no cross-round learning through retained updates.

BoundaryThe calculation cannot establish identification of a real channel effect; absence of cross-round memory does not cancel this round’s effect.

Mathematical construction: shared input can masquerade as feedbackTeaching scenario

AssumptionsVariables and intervention meanings are fully stipulated, with U affecting both endpoints; the comparison removes only R’s information to the receiver.

Let external variable U be 0 or 1, alarm R=U, and subsequent action Y=U. Observation shows R=Y, but cutting only the alarm connection while preserving U and the action rule leaves Y equal to U. Alarm and action share a source; observed correlation does not establish that R causes Y. Changing the actual rule to Y=R creates another model and cannot be done silently after results.

BoundaryWhether shared inputs, substitute channels, or intervention side effects actually exist requires material and is not prejudged by this example.

Maryland renewals: process changes and complete channel identification are separateDocumented case

Maryland’s health department’s 2024 report recalls CMS clarification in August 2023 that renewals based on existing data should occur at the individual rather than household level. The state subsequently records system changes and explicitly states that the updated process entered actual use in November 2023. This section adds the location of material between problem return and subsequent execution: receipt of a report alone does not establish an effect, while recorded actual process changes should not be erased.

What does not follow

  • Parameter blockage in a formal model can be calculated exactly but does not automatically validate real channels or experimental implementability.
  • Measuring one state change this round does not additionally establish channel capacity, reliability, costs, or long-term effects.
  • Negative or oscillating results may also contain effective feedback; effective does not mean beneficial.
  • Failure to pass the positive criterion may reflect counterevidence or insufficient measurement; record them separately rather than treating uncertainty as proof of zero effect.

Scope and open questions

The actual administrative report distinguishes problem return, system change, and actual use without pretending to provide certification by a complete channel-effect test; transient control and common causes use separate explicit constructions.

6.2.1Feedback Delay and the Stability Interval ​

In briefWith the same corrective strength, a later response may be more prone to repeated overshoot. Rather than an empirical slogan that ‘delay is dangerous’, this section calculates an exact stability range in a small model with fully disclosed assumptions.

A local model that can be analyzed on its own is x_{t+1}=x_t−k x_{t−d}. Here x_t is the signed, dimensionless deviation from the target, k is a fixed real-valued gain, and d is a fixed nonnegative integer delay. The sampling interval is fixed. The model excludes external shocks, measurement noise, saturation in execution, and state bounds. For every finite initial history, the zero solution is asymptotically stable if and only if 0<k<2sin[π/(4d+2)]. Equality at the bounds is outside the stability interval. The proof is in Appendix C.10.

For example, let k=0.8 and set every entry in the initial history to 1. The model is asymptotically stable at delays of 0 or 1 step and unstable at delays of 2 or 3 steps. In all four cases the first step takes the value from 1 to 0.2. With the channel blocked at k=0, the value stays at 1. The model thus exhibits both effective feedback and failure of stability. Crossing the stability boundary means that a nondecaying or growing mode exists. It does not imply that every trajectory, including the one with zero initial history, grows.

Stability does not guarantee that the deviation shrinks at every step, that transient peaks are acceptable, or that execution costs are affordable. A negative x_t indicates only that the target has been overshot. It does not represent a negative number of tasks. The equation does not model nonnegativity, demand, heterogeneous service, strategic responses, or permissions in real queues. Independent measurement and model validation are needed before applying this criterion to a real process. The criterion must not be used to set a real-world corrective gain that has not been identified.

6.2.1Note

Understanding this section

6.2.1 Feedback Delay and Stability Intervals

With the same corrective strength, a later response may be more prone to repeated overshoot. Rather than an empirical slogan that ‘delay is dangerous’, this section calculates an exact stability range in a small model with fully disclosed assumptions.

The model is x_{t+1}=x_t−k x_{t−d}. x is signed, dimensionless deviation from a target; k is a fixed real gain; d is a fixed nonnegative integer delay; sampling intervals are fixed. Given a finite initial history x_{−d},…,x_0, the subsequent trajectory is unique. There are no external shocks, measurement noise, actuator saturation, or state boundaries. Negative x means crossing the target, not a negative task count.

The result proved is that the zero solution is asymptotically stable for all finite initial histories if and only if 0<k<k_c(d), where k_c(d)=2sin[π/(4d+2)]. Asymptotic stability requires small deviations not to escape control as they evolve and to tend to zero in the long run; for this finite-dimensional fixed linear system, it is characterized by every characteristic root having modulus strictly below 1. This is not selecting one attractive initial trajectory or merely observing decline for a few steps.

Store current and delayed states together as z_t=(x_t,x_{t−1},…,x_{t−d}), giving fixed-matrix recurrence z_{t+1}=Az_t. Substituting mode x_t=λ^t yields characteristic polynomial p(λ,k)=λ^{d+1}−λ^d+k. If all roots lie inside the unit circle, every mode decays; even with repeated roots, polynomial factors in t multiplied by an exponential with base strictly below 1 tend to zero. A root with modulus ≥1 supplies a nondecaying or growing mode for a corresponding real initial history, violating ‘all histories tend to zero’.

First exclude k≤0. At k=0 there is a root 1, and any nonzero constant history persists, so asymptotic stability fails. For k<0, p(1,k)=k<0, while p>0 for sufficiently large positive λ, so continuity gives at least one real root λ>1. For d=0, directly use x_{t+1}=(1−k)x_t: |1−k|<1 is exactly 0<k<2.

For d≥1 and sufficiently small positive k, the root 1 at k=0 is simple and implicit differentiation shows inward motion λ=1−k+O(k²); the other d roots start near 0 and remain inside by continuity. Thus a stable small-positive-gain interval exists. Finding its endpoint requires locating the first contact of characteristic roots with the unit circle, not merely running several floating-point trials.

Let a boundary root be λ=e^{iθ}, 0<θ<2π. From p=0, k=λ^d(1−λ)=2sin(θ/2)exp{i[(d+1/2)θ−π/2]}. Since sin(θ/2)>0, positive real k requires the phase to be an integer multiple of 2π, giving θ=(π+4πm)/(2d+1), m=0,…,d. Among all possible positive boundaries, the minimum 2sin(θ/2) comes from the smallest angle θ=π/(2d+1) and its conjugate, yielding k_c=2sin[π/(4d+2)]. Roots vary continuously with k and remain bounded on finite parameter intervals; leaving the unit circle requires crossing one of these boundaries, so stability holds for 0<k<k_c.

Necessity also requires ruling out “leaving and then returning.” At the boundary, p_λ=λ^{d−1}[(d+1)λ−d] is nonzero, since ((d+1)λ=d) requires |λ|=d/(d+1)<1. Every unit-circle root is therefore simple. Differentiating p=0 gives λ′/λ=(λ−1)/{k[(d+1)λ−d]}. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate and taking real parts yields numerator real part (2d+1)(1−cosθ), hence d log|λ|/dk=(2d+1)(1−cosθ)/{k|(d+1)e^{iθ}−d|²}>0. Every positive-gain crossing goes outward, with no inward reentry, so complete stability cannot return above the first boundary. d=0 was already handled directly.

At k=k_c, at least one root has unit modulus, yielding a nondecaying mode, so equality is excluded. A numerical value 0.999999… caused by rounding cannot justify inclusion. Beyond the boundary, a growing mode exists, but not every history grows: an all-zero history stays zero, and special histories containing no unstable mode may behave differently. “System instability” concerns the family of all histories; it does not mean every curve diverges.

Fix k=0.8. For d=0,1,2,3, critical values are respectively 2,1, approximately 0.618034 and 0.445042: the first two are stable and the latter two unstable. If every required initial-history value is 1, the first step is always 1−0.8=0.2. Under complete blockage k=0, the trajectory stays 1. Return thus produces a first-step difference of 0.8 while long-term stability differs, showing that “has an effect” and “stable” are nonequivalent.

More closely, d=1 gives first updates 0.2,−0.6,−0.76: despite asymptotic stability, absolute deviation can increase between adjacent steps and overshoot occurs. Stability guarantees neither stepwise decrease, reaching arbitrary tolerance within a finite window, safe transient peaks, nor affordable execution costs. The figures show only model calculations for t=0…24; the long-term conclusion comes from proof, not visual inspection of curves.

Actual use separately requires checking error definitions, sampling frequency, fixed versus varying delay, actuator saturation, service constraints, external inputs, and strategic human responses. Real queues have nonnegative task counts and heterogeneous service and demand; institutional correction also involves authority and costs. None is modeled by this equation. This section therefore cannot prescribe k=0.8 directly for an actual process.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Disclose the model assumptions: signed deviation, fixed gain/delay, finite initial history, and absence of noise/constraints.

  2. 2

    Extend to a finite-dimensional linear state and explain the equivalence between all roots strictly inside the unit circle and decay for all histories.

  3. 3

    Use root 1 and a real root greater than 1 to exclude k≤0, and solve d=0 separately.

  4. 4

    Prove stability for sufficiently small positive k, then set a unit-circle root e^{iθ} to find the first positive boundary.

  5. 5

    Derive θ and k_c from the positive-real phase condition, using root continuity to establish stability before the first boundary.

  6. 6

    Implicitly differentiate boundary roots and prove all positive-k crossings go outward, ruling out renewed stability.

  7. 7

    Exclude equality and distinguish existence of unstable modes from growth of every trajectory; substitute the four d values to check numerical values.

  8. 8

    Compare first-step blockage and feedback, then assess effect, asymptotic stability, transient metrics, and actual adoption separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Effective feedback

Compared with blockage, return has changed a subsequent state.

≠

Asymptotic stability

Every finite initial history tends to zero over time and satisfies this linear stability property.

System instability

A nondecaying or growing mode exists.

≠

Every trajectory diverges

A much stronger, false claim; zero history is a counterexample.

Asymptotic convergence to zero

A property over sufficiently long time.

≠

Improvement at every step and acceptable peaks

Separate finite-time tasks and constraints.

Signed deviation

Negative values mean overshooting the target.

≠

Actual task count

Usually has separate nonnegativity constraints and cannot be directly equated with deviation.

Mathematical construction: four delays share the first step but differ afterwardTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPure mathematical calculation without external inputs, noise, saturation, or state boundaries. Initial histories are completely specified for each d.

Let k=0.8 and all initial-history values required by each delay be 1. For t=0…4, d=0 gives 1,0.2,0.04,0.008,0.0016; d=1 gives 1,0.2,−0.6,−0.76,−0.28; d=2 gives 1,0.2,−0.6,−1.4,−1.56; d=3 gives 1,0.2,−0.6,−1.4,−2.2. Each value follows the preceding recursion; for example, at d=2, x₃=x₂−0.8x₀=−0.6−0.8=−1.4. The figure shows every integer step through t=24 under the same assumptions, with a step-by-step calculation CSV.

BoundaryFinite trajectories do not replace the necessary-and-sufficient proof above and are not device or organizational measurements.

Mathematical construction: stable does not mean better at every stepTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll-one initial history. Absolute error and the t=2 threshold are explicit teaching tasks, not real safety thresholds.

For d=1, k=0.8 lies in 0<k<1. x₁=0.2 and x₂=−0.6, so |x₂|=0.6>|x₁|=0.2: stepwise decrease fails. A predetermined task requiring absolute deviation≤0.1 at t=2 also fails. Asymptotic convergence cannot rewrite that deadline requirement.

BoundaryEvaluate eventual convergence, meeting deadlines, transient peaks, and costs separately.

Mathematical construction: the boundary and zero historyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFully specified recursion and initial values; no actual experiment.

For d=0 and k=2, x_{t+1}=−x_t; starting at x₀=1 gives 1,−1,1,−1, never tending to zero, showing why equality is excluded. Although d=2 and k=0.8 exceed the critical value, setting x_{−2}=x_{−1}=x₀=0 keeps the recursion at 0, showing that instability does not mean growth of every trajectory.

BoundaryZero history cannot establish system stability, while one nondecaying history suffices to refute “all histories tend to zero.”

What it limitsThe same model may grow later; fixed 0.8 exceeds this delay's critical 0.618034.

What does not follow

  • The stability region is a strictly open interval, excluding both endpoints k=0 and k=k_c.
  • A finite trajectory alone cannot prove asymptotic stability for all histories. Root analysis and crossing direction provide that proof.
  • The criterion applies only to fixed discrete delay and fixed real gain. Time-varying delay, random disturbances, nonlinearities, and saturation require new analysis.
  • A within-model return effect is not certification by an empirical channel-effect test and supplies no authority for actual action.
  • The four trajectory panels share a horizontal axis but label vertical ranges separately. Visual slopes cannot be used to compare magnitudes across panels.

Scope and open questions

This is a mathematical proposition under complete assumptions. Proof and reproducible trajectories best show the nonequivalence; no real organization is forced into the role of a verified case of this equation.

Do d=1 and k=1 satisfy strict asymptotic stability?

No. The critical value is 1, equality is excluded, and a nondecaying mode exists.

Why does finding the first unit-circle intersection not yet prove instability for every larger k?

One must also rule out roots crossing inward again. The always-positive boundary radial derivative does this.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

For d=3 and k=0.8, does an all-zero initial history remaining zero refute instability?

No. Instability means some nondecaying/growing modes exist, not that every history grows.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does the d=1 sequence from 0.2 to −0.6 contradict asymptotic stability?

No contradiction: asymptotic stability does not require absolute error to decrease stepwise.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If an actual processing queue has a measured average delay of 2 steps, may control parameters directly use k<0.618034?

No. Average delay is not fixed delay. Nonnegative tasks, service constraints, shocks, and execution authority are also unverified; independent modeling and risk analysis are required.

6.3Feedback-Mediated Learning (CM-LEARNING) ​

In briefHearing feedback yesterday and changing something today does not establish future use. Feedback-mediated learning traces what changed, what retains it, whether it was actually used later, and where the predetermined task consequently differs.

Basic grounds: the “Effective Feedback” mechanism (§6.2). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Feedback-mediated learning requires a return to cause an update that can be retained and is actually used in a subsequent task. It has two branches, each requiring its own evidence: the carrier branch, transmitted through a current carrier, and the historical-increment branch, which claims a historical increment beyond the current representation. They correspond respectively to the carrier-transmission route and the historical-increment route of §4.5.

The carrier branch. Its enabling conditions begin with effective feedback changing an internal state, parameter, rule, memory, or structure that can be located. A specified carrier retains the update or sustains continued updating, and the update is actually used in repeated rounds. The later task, fixed in advance, shows a reviewable difference relative to a baseline or an alternative process stated in advance. A causal claim must have interruption, replacement, recovery, or a comparison that meets the conditions for identification, and must address common inputs, continued training, selection, attrition, and changes in measurement. A claim about transfer or predictive gain also requires evaluation suited to that claim, using an independent task or out-of-sample data. The mechanism chain is:

Effective feedback → locatable internal update → retention or continued updating through the update carrier → actual use in later rounds → change in the outcome of the prespecified task

A single parameter change, a single success, a single write-back, or the archiving of materials is insufficient to establish this learning mechanism. Write-back means that feedback changes rules, records, resources, or roles, and the change is actually carried out. The corresponding mechanism claim is not supported if the update is not retained, if it is not used later, if a common input alone can explain the task outcome, or if only a proxy measure changes while the task fixed in advance is unaffected. Effective feedback, learning in general, transfer across contexts, and net benefit need to be judged separately. Established learning does not imply improvement, a unified goal, or authorization to act.

When the goal itself changes, the reasons for forming the new goal and the decision procedure should be stated. The results, failures, and costs under the old goal should be preserved before a comparison is established for the new task. A goal reconstructed later must not be used to rewrite failure on the old task as success (see §2.14).

Learning in general can be supported by evidence from the relevant domain, such as new tasks that can be completed repeatedly, skills that are retained and used, or traceable teaching or organizational processes. It need not first be formally determined, under this framework, to be a case of this mechanism. A report may state together that “the practice has changed,” “the subsequent net effect remains undetermined,” and “the feedback-mediated mechanism has yet to be identified,” without collapsing these judgments into a single “pass” or “fail.” 〔Studies 16.02, 25.01–25.08, 31.08〕

Learning evaluation should also distinguish task completion with support, independent transfer after support is withdrawn, and subsequent outcomes in everyday life. Necessary support can form part of an expressive or collaborative task. In that case, failure without support does not negate an earlier success. If independent transfer was the original goal, testing it requires a comparison suited to that goal with support withdrawn. Responsibilities for choosing the goal, confirming retention of the update, measuring task performance, and judging net benefit are separate. Continuing support must not be used to deny a functional gain, and performance with assistance must not stand in for independent skill.

The historical-increment branch. In addition to carrier updates, repeated use, and a task comparison, there must be a historical-increment test that supports an additional historical conditional increment relative to an explicitly stated current representation. When the current carrier has sufficiently retained what has been learned, this increment can disappear while learning in the carrier branch still holds. Known current carriers must not be omitted to manufacture an increment. Branches must not be switched after the results are seen to rescue the original test. The two routes each state their own comparisons, counterexamples, and failure conditions.

6.3Note

Understanding this section

6.3 Feedback-mediated learning (CM-LEARNING)

Hearing feedback yesterday and changing something today does not establish future use. Feedback-mediated learning traces what changed, what retains it, whether it was actually used later, and where the predetermined task consequently differs.

The basic ground is the “Effective Feedback” mechanism (§6.2): return from a prior state or output actually causes change; the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) provide review methods. Only then ask whether the update is locatable, retainable, and later used. A before/after comparison of system operation alone cannot distinguish feedback learning from continued external training, member replacement, or changed measurement.

The carrier branch has five stages: effective feedback → internal update → carrier retention or continuous updating → actual use in subsequent rounds → changed predetermined task results. Updates may reside in parameters, rules, memory, structure, or other internal states, not only readable archives. Retention may depend on continued maintenance rather than a one-time immutable write. The key is specifying location, version, sequence, and the use path.

Minimum material must connect pre/post-update states, carrier maintenance, repeated use, and task comparisons. Causal explanation additionally requires proportionate interruption, replacement, restoration, or comparisons meeting identification conditions, addressing shared inputs, continued training, selection, attrition, and measurement changes. All comparisons follow targets and permitted operations. Necessary support must not be removed, nor people forcibly intervened upon, merely to validate the theory. Cross-context transfer or out-of-sample predictive-gain claims require proportionate independent-task or out-of-sample material.

One parameter change, one success, one write-back, and archiving each cover only part of the chain. If updates are not retained or later used, shared inputs explain results, or only proxy scores improve without changing the predetermined task, the corresponding learning mechanism lacks support. Report where the chain breaks. Uncertain net effects do not establish no learning, and changed practices do not establish every mechanism.

Beyond the carrier chain, the historical-increment branch asks whether past history adds explanation or prediction of predetermined subsequent outcomes conditional on an explicitly stated current representation, supported by an eligible historical-increment test (§4.5). Carrier-mediated learning may be fully retained in current parameters, leaving no need for extra history without canceling what was learned. Conversely, useful historical variables alone do not establish the whole return–update–retention–use chain.

The two routes therefore need separately declared comparisons, counterexamples, and failure conditions beforehand. Known current parameters cannot be deleted to manufacture historical increments. Missing use evidence on the carrier route cannot be rescued by saying “history matters,” nor can failed historical-increment checks prompt retrospective switching of the primary criterion. The carrier route may hold independently, but through its own material, not the room left by another branch's failure.

Ordinary learning need not wait for this framework's formal certification. Repeatable new-task performance, retained skills, or traceable teaching/organizational processes within a domain may support learning judgments within their respective scopes. “The practice has changed,” “the feedback-mediated mechanism is insufficiently identified,” and “subsequent net benefit remains uncertain” can all be reported without contradiction. Missing framework eligibility does not erase independent facts; domain conclusions do not automatically establish every framework mechanism either.

Established learning does not mean improvement and creates neither a unified objective nor authority to act. Changed targets require public reasons and decision procedures, retention of failures, results, and costs under old targets, and a new comparison for the new task. Retrospectively renaming the original mistaken task “exploration” cannot declare success.

Also distinguish supported completion, independent transfer after support withdrawal, and subsequent life outcomes. Necessary support may constitute part of a collaborative/expression task, in which case failure without it does not cancel prior supported success. If the predetermined target is independent transfer, assisted performance cannot masquerade as independent capability. Whether support must remain, target selection is reasonable, updates persist, performance improves, and net benefits arise each carries its own evidential responsibility.

If learning changes the target, explain under §2.14 who proposes reopening, which new material or omissions justify it, and who decides, while retaining results and costs under the old target. If training later shifts to another occupation, for example, learning on the new task can be evaluated, but failure at the original occupational task cannot become success of the original plan. Ordinary skill formation, current-carrier transmission, and additional historical increments remain separate judgments.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify the task, baseline, window, and support conditions, then locate effective return and the internal states it changes.

  2. 2

    Trace update-carrier versions, retention/continuous updating, and repeated later use. Archiving cannot replace use.

  3. 3

    Compare predetermined task outcomes and check shared inputs, continued training, selection, attrition, and measurement changes.

  4. 4

    Transfer or predictive-gain claims require separate independent-task/out-of-sample evaluation. Comparisons must not cause unauthorized interruption of support.

  5. 5

    Separate carrier and historical-increment routes beforehand. The latter additionally requires a historical-increment test relative to a fully explicit current representation.

  6. 6

    Independently retain evidence of ordinary learning and changed organizational practices, while closing specific mechanisms and net benefits separately.

  7. 7

    Changed targets retain the old task's accounting and initiate new comparisons. Acquired function, independent transfer, later life outcomes, and authority are not merged.

Distinctions to keep clear

Update retention

The carrier retains or continuously maintains the update into later windows.

≠

Actual use

Later tasks actually read and use it; storage is not use.

Carrier-based learning

The current carrier takes up the update and affects later tasks.

≠

Additional historical increment

History still supplies a conditional increment given the current representation; a historical-increment test is additionally required.

Supported performance

Completion with tools or collaborative support under the original task arrangement.

≠

Independent transfer

Completion under explicitly specified support-withdrawal/new-context conditions. The two cannot masquerade as each other.

Task difference

A reviewable change in the predetermined task outcome.

≠

Net benefit

A separate judgment combining objectives, costs, risks, and distribution.

Mathematical construction: feedback writes a parameter, and later use yields calculable differencesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTarget, training and update rules, test inputs, and carrier replacement are all artificial assumptions. No other external inputs or parameter changes occur. There is one training round and two subsequent use rounds.

A fictional predictor outputs y=θu, initially θ=0, with target rule y*=2u. In training round u=1, actual output is 0; comparing against target 2 returns error e=2−0=2, and θ←θ+e writes parameter 2. Training then stops; θ is retained and actually used in two new rounds u=2 and u=3, yielding outputs 4 and 6 with squared errors 0 and 0. The baseline retaining old θ=0 outputs 0 and 0, with squared errors 16 and 36. Replacing the carrier with θ=0 only before use restores errors 16 and 36; restoring θ=2 returns them to 0 and 0. The complete model connects return, update, retention, use, and task differences.

BoundaryThis is a mathematically computable construction, not an actual machine experiment. Different test inputs do not establish arbitrary real-world generalization across contexts or constitute a formal test.

Mathematical construction: learning retained in the current state, with zero historical incrementTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe output rule is fixed and deterministic; θ contains all callable learned content in this example, and the comparison model may read it.

Continue with the predictor. The complete current record includes θ=2 and input u, so the output must be 2u. Whatever the number or ordering of earlier training rounds, histories ending in the same θ give identical future outputs; additional history cannot reduce an already zero prediction error. Carrier learning is therefore compatible with disappearance of an additional historical increment. If the current representation is deliberately changed to “whether the parameter is nonzero,” θ=1 and θ=2 collapse together, and history may help distinguish them. This coarsening must be disclosed; a known θ cannot be deleted while pretending that no current carrier exists.

BoundaryWhether an actual carrier is sufficient requires evidence; sufficiency in this construction cannot be directly generalized.

Teaching construction: supported and independent tasks are different examinationsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA purely teaching scenario, with no actual participants, measurements, or support-withdrawal trial; whether the code table is available is declared before evaluation.

A fictional decoding task permits a code table, and a participant correctly completes three decodings. If the original target was “complete with the table,” the table cannot suddenly be removed and failure used to cancel the original success. If the original target was “decode independently without the table,” the first three performances do not establish it. This example only illustrates the evaluation arrangement; three performances alone do not prove feedback-mediated learning or retained updates.

BoundaryThis does not advocate withdrawing necessary support in reality; independent comparisons must account for ethics, risks, and permissions.

Mathematical construction: rewriting a target cannot erase failure on the old taskTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe two targets and shared output are constructed; the new target is not presumed inherently wrong or right.

If the original target requires output 2 and the actual output is 3, squared loss is (3−2)²=1. Setting a new target of 3 afterward makes the new task's loss 0, but the original task's loss remains 1. The new target also requires a reasonable formation process and subsequent comparisons. Changing the numbers changes the evaluation question, not the past output.

BoundarySuccess under a new target cannot remove the old target's failure record, costs, or responsibility.

Maryland's new renewal process: starting use still differs from long-term learningDocumented case

The 2024 Maryland report explicitly records use of the updated ex parte renewal process beginning in November 2023 and states that future renewals will continue using the modifications. This section adds the evidential tense distinction between “already used” and “will continue to be used”: the former is an implementation fact reported in the document, the latter a prospective arrangement. A future plan alone cannot establish multi-round retention, stable use, or long-term net effects.

What does not follow

  • Effective feedback whose update resets each round may have a one-time effect without cross-round learning through that carrier.
  • Additional historical increments may be zero when the current carrier is sufficient; learning does not disappear thereby.
  • Deleting a known parameter within a model creates insufficient representation. Concealing that deletion cannot justify claiming that history is ontologically irreducible.
  • When support belongs to the original task, unsupported failure cannot cancel supported success. Independent transfer still requires its own comparison.
  • Mere evidence insufficiency remains unresolved; reject a specific claim only with proportionate counterevidence. Unknown long-term net benefit is not zero learning of every kind.

Scope and open questions

Actual implementation records help distinguish material on updates, completed use, and future continuation. The mathematical example fully discloses its assumed mechanism, without retroactively granting an administrative report the status of a formal learning case.

6.4A Hypothetical Appeal Illustrating Feedback, Institutional Write-Back, and Learning ​

In briefThe same appeal may stop at “received,” change the case status, be implemented, or even influence processing across later rounds. Every additional level of claim adds an evidential responsibility; one acknowledgment cannot cross every step.

Suppose a hypothetical institution receives an appeal. This example illustrates the method of classification only. It draws on no real-world material and provides no external empirical proof.

The appeal is received and a receipt is generated. Records, rules, resources, roles, responsibilities, memory, and stopping conditions all remain unchanged. This is signal arrival alone, with neither effective feedback nor institutional write-back.

The appeal changes the case-status item through a specified channel, but the change is not put into effect. This can be effective feedback in the sense of the definition (§3.3) while still falling short of complete institutional write-back in the sense of the human-domain clause “Institutional Write-Back” (§7.1).

The change in that item is put into effect, and intake, the change, execution, and duration are all recorded. This is an institutional write-back. The fact of write-back does not establish that the institution is justified, nor does it amount to long-term repair.

When the write-back produces an update to a rule or state that can be retained, the update enters several later rounds of similar cases, and a corresponding task comparison and causal basis are available, a candidate for carrier feedback-mediated learning may be proposed, that is, a candidate in the carrier branch. If a historical conditional increment beyond the current state is also claimed, a historical-increment test tests it independently.

Thus, neither feedback nor write-back amounts to learning. The evidence requirements increase from one of the three to the next. Having an appeal entry point or making a public response cannot satisfy them all at once.

6.4Note

Understanding this section

6.4 A Fictional Appeal Example of Feedback, Institutional Write-Back, and Learning

The same appeal may stop at “received,” change the case status, be implemented, or even influence processing across later rounds. Every additional level of claim adds an evidential responsibility; one acknowledgment cannot cross every step.

The original text explicitly posits a fictional institution, so the following teaches classification rather than reporting an actual appeal or providing external empirical proof. We fix the same object, appeal, and observation window, varying subsequent conditions to see how far a claim may go. This is not a maturation ladder that real institutions necessarily follow.

In the first scenario, the appeal is received and an acknowledgment generated, while the stated records, rules, resources, roles, responsibilities, memory, and stopping conditions all remain unchanged. The acknowledgment establishes signal arrival, not automatic change in any relevant subsequent item. Define acknowledgment metadata and the institutional elements in question beforehand. If an actual acknowledgment itself triggers scheduling or stopping conditions, it is no longer this example's “all unchanged” case; actual channels and effects require rechecking.

In the second scenario, the appeal changes the case-status item through a specified channel, but execution has not begun. Given proportionate causal comparison, this can satisfy the return effect in the definition of effective feedback (§3.3): the status item is also a subsequent state, and feedback need not await a changed final outcome. The human-domain clause “Institutional Write-Back” (§7.1), however, requires change in that item and actual execution, so complete institutional write-back cannot yet be claimed. That item changing later in time is not itself evidence that “the appeal caused it.”

The third scenario carries the change in that item into actual execution, separately recording acceptance, the item's before/after versions, execution, and duration, satisfying the example's write-back classification. Duration is part of the classification conditions; one execution does not imply permanent validity. The “Institutional Write-Back” clause is a classification rule, not an abstract empirical truth or permission to alter an institution. The conclusion rule “Institutional Write-Back” (§4.13.4) additionally requires a channel-effect test to locate the specified feedback channel, and a comparison under the definition of effective feedback. Successful classification and complete empirical-mechanism support must not be conflated.

The fourth scenario additionally requires a retainable rule or state update, actual use in multiple later rounds of similar cases, prespecified task comparisons, and corresponding causal grounds before a carrier-based feedback-mediated learning candidate can be proposed. One write-back does not automatically establish preservation and use across rounds. Repeated identical later outcomes may also arise from continuing external instructions or shared environments; proportionate competing explanations must be excluded. A further claim of an additional historical increment beyond the current state is tested separately by a historical-increment test.

In this example, evidence requirements increase with claim strength, but this does not mean learning in every domain must first pass through institutional write-back. The fixed route here is “how an appeal changes an institution and affects later cases.” Learning generally may occur in other carriers, assessed separately under 6.3. Diagram arrows also do not guarantee that receipt eventually leads to learning; every connection may stop.

A write-back fact guarantees neither institutional justification nor long-term repair. Executing an improper rule may still involve actual changes in institutional elements and implementation; record facts and normative issues separately. A rule's unjustified character cannot erase effects that occurred, and successful execution cannot endorse its justification. Repair targets, responsibility, authorization, and implementation procedures remain separate judgments.

For actual material, list “already occurred,” “insufficient evidence,” and “plan only” individually. An open entry point, public response, change in case status, actual execution, retained use, and task effects each have their place. Missing execution evidence cannot justify inventing implementation, while missing long-term material cannot deny an evidenced short-term change. Teaching tables merely organize material; entering “yes” is not the material itself.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Declare this to be the author's fictional classification example; fix the object, the relevant items, time window, and appeal route without fabricating an actual case.

  2. 2

    First check arrival/acknowledgment, then the change in that item caused by the specified return; do not merge the two.

  3. 3

    A change in that item with proportionate return comparison may constitute feedback. If it has not entered execution, stop there without upgrading to complete write-back.

  4. 4

    After actual execution, separately record acceptance, versions, execution, and duration, classifying under the “Institutional Write-Back” clause while separately checking causal-mechanism eligibility.

  5. 5

    Only after checking retention, multi-round use, prespecified task comparisons, and causal material should a carrier-learning candidate be proposed.

  6. 6

    If an additional historical increment is claimed, run a historical-increment test independently; do not make it a mandatory condition for every write-back or learning claim.

  7. 7

    Finally distinguish write-back facts, learning, long-term repair, justification, and permissions, locating gaps at specific levels.

Distinctions to keep clear

Acceptance / acknowledgment

Confirms arrival or the start of processing.

≠

Case-status change

Requires locating before/after differences in the relevant items and checking their source.

Effective feedback

A specified return produces differences in subsequent states or related quantities.

≠

Complete institutional write-back

This example additionally requires changes in institutional elements to enter actual execution, with duration recorded.

One write-back

The modification in this round has been implemented.

≠

Carrier-based learning

A retainable update is repeatedly used later and changes the prespecified task.

Classification under the “Institutional Write-Back” clause

Distinguishes acceptance, modification, and execution under given rules.

≠

Empirical support or authorization

Requires corresponding evidence or norms/procedures; classification cannot replace them.

Teaching construction: distinguishing four versions item by itemTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEntirely constructed. B's rule explicitly states s=1 with this return and s=0 without it, holding other conditions fixed. The flags are given model states, not certification produced by filling out a real-world form.

A fictional system defines case status s=0 as awaiting the original process and s=1 as entering review. It also records actual execution e, rule retention p, and subsequent use count n. Version A only receives the appeal, with s=0, e=0, p=0, n=0: arrival only. Version B changes s to 1 under the given return rule, but e=0: state feedback within the model, without complete write-back. Version C adds review execution e=1 to B, recording acceptance, status change, execution time, and a two-day validity period: it permits a one-time write-back classification. Version D additionally retains the update p=1, uses it in three later similar cases n=3, and adds task and causal comparisons: only then does the material reach the level needed to propose a carrier-learning candidate.

BoundaryEven D cannot establish an actual mechanism merely from p=1 and n=3; corresponding actual material is required, and neither additional history nor net benefit has thereby been proved.

Mathematical construction: task comparison needs explicit rulesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsInputs, targets, both rule versions, and the meaning of replacement are artificially fixed; no shared external instruction changes outputs.

Continue with version D. For all three new cases, the prespecified task is correct entry into review, with ideal output y*=1. The old rule outputs 0 for all three specified inputs; the new retained rule outputs 1. Old mean squared loss is [(0−1)²×3]/3=1; new loss is 0. In the model, replacing only the rule with the old version before use returns loss to 1; restoring the new rule returns it to 0. This provides a computable connection between use and outcome. “Used three times” without these comparisons cannot directly count as success.

BoundaryThe model contains no actual case rights, resource costs, or legal effects; it cannot adjudicate an actual institution.

Teaching construction: an acknowledgment may trigger an effect, but the question must changeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn explicit conditional counterfactual, not a description of any current appeal system; 24 hours is a teaching assumption.

A fictional system stipulates that generating a receipt acknowledgment pauses the case-deadline clock for 24 hours. If this rule is actually executed, a stopping condition has changed, so the case cannot remain in version A, where “all relevant items remain unchanged.” State the changed item and channel, distinguishing the clock pause from subsequent substantive review. The pause alone proves neither ultimate appeal success nor long-term learning.

BoundaryNot every actual acknowledgment can be presumed to suspend deadlines, and this provides no advice on legal time limits.

What counterexamples change

Sourced counterexampleOriginal fictional example A has only an acknowledgment; all relevant institutional elements remain unchanged.

What it limitsAn entry point or response alone cannot establish effective feedback and write-back.

What it limitsMissing evidence does not automatically mean an event was absent; distinguish verified nonexecution from non-observation.

What does not follow

  • This section has no actual appeal object; its constructed states, counts, and losses must not be treated as administrative statistics.
  • The successive added conditions here concern only the appeal route, not a claim that all learning depends on institutional write-back (§7.1).
  • A change in case status can coexist with lack of execution; incomplete final implementation cannot cancel evidenced state feedback.
  • One execution guarantees neither persistence, learning, repair, nor justification; duration cannot be left blank and then assumed permanent.
  • Knowing that no relevant change occurred differs from lacking material observing change. With insufficient material, retain unresolved status rather than treating missing records as absent events.

Scope and open questions

The original section explicitly teaches classification through a fictional institution. Its identity is retained and developed through conditional variants, without forcing in real historical facts or inventing appeal cases presented as real.
