6.5Maintenance and Preservation–Dissipation (CM-MAINTENANCE) ​

In briefA machine that keeps running or a service that stays open may depend on someone continuously replenishing, replacing, correcting, or clearing obstacles. Maintenance analysis identifies how those specific inputs preserve identity or function, while asking what is preserved, who bears the work, and whether a backup can actually take over when failure occurs.

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Basic state terms (§3.2) supply its domain restriction in state terms. Maintenance has three requirements. The current identity criterion or functional criterion is stated in advance, together with the maintenance time window. A channel-effect test must identify replenishment, replacement, correction, or removal as the specified channel that changes how identity or function continues to hold. The comparison also needs to cover maintenance, reduced maintenance, mismatched maintenance, and cessation of maintenance.

The mechanism chain is:

Wear, drift, loss, or component exit → specified maintenance channel → replenishment/replacement/correction/removal → change in how long identity or function holds or in the probability of failure

The maintenance mechanism has three branches. The current branch checks what effect maintenance inputs have on how the current identity or function continues to hold. The carrier-accumulation branch also uses §4.5 to check the current carrier of wear or capability, how previous inputs formed that carrier, how it is retained or replenished across time windows, and longitudinal and causal evidence that maintenance changes how identity or function holds later. The historical-increment branch is of the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test is added only when a historical conditional increment beyond the current representation is claimed. The maintenance claim should be narrowed or withdrawn in the following cases: the object continues to satisfy the identity criterion or functional criterion in the target time window without ongoing maintenance; a change in maintenance input makes no difference to the relevant outcome; or an independent shock can explain the supposed wear. The definition also fails if the old maintenance criteria are still used after the original identity criterion has changed.

A need for maintenance does not imply that an object should persist indefinitely. The existence of a maintenance channel cannot directly designate a specific party to take up the work, assign responsibility, or impose a duty to make sacrifices. Mismatched maintenance can prolong the period during which the old identity criterion holds while undermining the target functional criterion. An orderly stop, object conversion, or dissolution may also be outcomes the definition permits.

Maintenance analysis also needs to distinguish tasks during normal operation, migration, failure, and recovery. Interface standards specify conditions under which interoperability is possible. Actual compatibility still depends on implementation versions, business semantics, environment and load, testing, and on-site adaptation. The existence of parts does not imply that their specifications fit, their quality can be verified, personnel can reach the site, or personnel are authorized to shut the system down. Additional maintenance work can take place outside the original object and be supplied by users, households, outsourced workers, or other institutions. Central work orders and operational outputs alone cannot account for the total amount of maintenance.

Test redundancy against failure conditions. A count of backups alone is insufficient. Two paths may share a power source, software state, transport channel, supplier, operator, or approval node. They can substitute for each other in normal operation and still fail together during a fault. Spare capacity, exposure to common causes, the time needed to switch, on-site skills, and the actual authority to switch should be verified separately. The communications, roads, fuel, spare parts, and personnel on which recovery depends should be included in the same time window. Adding backups, reducing coupling, and retaining independent local operation are only candidates. Their net effects depend on the specific failure and the cost of maintenance.

6.5Note

Understanding this section

6.5 Maintenance and preservation–dissipation (CM-MAINTENANCE)

A machine that keeps running or a service that stays open may depend on someone continuously replenishing, replacing, correcting, or clearing obstacles. Maintenance analysis identifies how those specific inputs preserve identity or function, while asking what is preserved, who bears the work, and whether a backup can actually take over when failure occurs.

The basic grounds are structural object (§3.1) and channel effect (§4.4): first specify the complete definition of the object, in which the identity criterion is only one item, then identify the specified maintenance channel. Basic state terms (§3.2) bound state terms such as persistence, disintegration, and repair, while the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) review explanations and evidence. Declare the current identity criterion or functional criterion and the window in advance to determine what maintenance preserves. ‘It still seems to be there’ does not automatically mean every function is normal.

The mechanism chain is wear, drift, loss, or component exit → specified maintenance channel → replenishment/replacement/correction/clearance → changed duration of identity or function preservation or failure probability. The result may extend usable time or change failure risk without returning the state to its initial value each time. Minimum comparison requires more than ‘a work order exists’: appropriate evidence across maintenance, reduced-maintenance, mismatched-maintenance, and stopping conditions, with a channel-effect test identifying the channel, is also needed. Real comparisons involving stopping maintenance are constrained by risk and authority; essential services cannot be arbitrarily shut down for verification.

The current branch asks about current inputs' effects on preserving identity or function within the current window. The carrier-accumulation branch additionally traces how earlier inputs form current wear or capability carriers, how they are retained/replenished across windows, and the longitudinal and causal grounds for maintenance changing subsequent preservation. The historical-increment branch asks about an additional historical increment: add a historical-increment test only when claiming that history has extra effects given the current representation. When current wear already sufficiently takes up the past, there may be no additional historical increment.

If an object satisfies the identity criterion or functional criterion without sustained maintenance within the target window, maintenance necessity cannot be extrapolated into that window. If changes to maintenance inputs do not change relevant outcomes, or supposed wear actually comes from an independent shock, narrow or withdraw the corresponding claim. If comparisons lack sensitivity, retain unresolved status rather than treating unmeasured differences as zero effects. Continuing to use an old criterion after the original identity criterion has changed conflates maintenance with object transformation; recheck the definition of the object.

A need for maintenance is not a normative reason for permanent persistence. A replenishment channel's existence does not automatically assign its burden to someone or create an obligation to sacrifice. Mismatched maintenance may keep the old identity criterion satisfied while damaging the target functional criterion; orderly stopping, transformation, or disintegration may also be permitted outcomes. Whether to maintain, toward which target, and who decides and executes remain questions for norms, authorization, and procedures. Technical feasibility does not imply obligation.

Normal operation, migration, failure, and recovery are different tasks. Interface standards describe conditions for possible interoperability; implementation versions, operational semantics, environmental loads, testing, and on-site adaptation determine actual compatibility in this instance. Parts in storage still require checking specifications, quality, transportation, on-site skills, and shutdown authority. ‘Exists’ cannot be collapsed into ‘usable in time.’ Replaceability under ordinary conditions also differs from completing replacement within an emergency window.

Maintenance may move outside the original object boundary and be supplied by users, families, outsourced workers, or other institutions. Fewer central work orders with maintained output need not mean less total maintenance labor. State where external burdens are borne, the workload, time, support, and right to stop. Only same-type quantities may be summed under explicit definitions; heterogeneous labor, risk, time, and rights must not be compressed into a unitless universal cost.

Redundancy must address failure conditions, not merely count backups. Two paths may share power, software state, transportation, suppliers, operators, or approval nodes. They may substitute for one another normally yet fail together during a fault. Check backup capacity, common-cause exposure, switching time, on-site skills, and actual switching authority separately; do not presume that two units mean independent reliability.

Recovery also depends on communications, roads, fuel, spare parts, and personnel, whose accessibility must be checked within the same failure window. If lost communications prevent obtaining switching permission, or blocked roads prevent parts from arriving, a backup on paper may not become actual recovery. Adding backups, reducing coupling, and retaining locally independent operation are all candidate designs; their net effects still depend on failure types, maintenance costs, and specific tasks.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix the complete definition of the object, the identity criterion and functional criterion, window, and normal/migration/failure/recovery task, avoiding conflation of identity and function.

  2. 2

    Locate the wear carrier, maintenance input, and effect path; predefine outcomes such as preservation duration or failure probability.

  3. 3

    Identify channels using appropriate maintenance, reduced-maintenance, mismatch, and stopping comparisons, addressing independent shocks, selection, and measurement limitations.

  4. 4

    State current, carrier-cumulative, and additional historical-increment branches separately; only the last additionally requires a historical-increment test.

  5. 5

    Check actual interface compatibility, part quality and arrival, personnel skills, and shutdown/switching authority, not just inventory.

  6. 6

    Include externally taken-up labor and recovery dependencies within the boundary; give explicit definitions for same-type quantities and list heterogeneous costs separately.

  7. 7

    Evaluate redundancy against common failure conditions and switching deadlines; then separately deliberate on whether to maintain, replace/stop, and assign responsibility and authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Preserving the identity criterion

The object continues to satisfy the declared identity criterion.

≠

Preserve F

Continue to meet specific functional requirements; the two can diverge.

A backup exists

Another component or path is present.

≠

Usable during failure

Capacity, common exposure, switching, arrival on site, and authority all fit the current window.

Standard interface

Specifies types and rules for possible interoperability.

≠

Actual compatibility

A usable connection under specific implementations, semantics, environments, and loads.

Maintenance is necessary

Function depends on certain inputs within a specified scope.

≠

Someone must continue bearing the burden

Still requires norms, responsibility, and authority; it does not follow directly.

Mathematical construction: maintenance changes preservation time; windows must not be swappedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsWear and compensation use the same units, rules are fixed, and there are no additional shocks. Only F is compared; this single variable is not claimed to validate the complete definition of the object or its identity criterion.

A fictional device starts with wear w₀=0, gains 2 per step, and receives maintenance input m that offsets wear, following w_{t+1}=max(0,w_t+2−m). Predefined function F requires w≤3 at every inspection time. No maintenance, m=0, gives 0,2,4, first failing at step two; reduced maintenance, m=1, gives 0,1,2,3,4, first failing at step four; maintenance m=2 keeps wear at 0 and preserves F throughout the chosen four-step window. If the task window is only the first step, all three satisfy F. Differences over a longer window cannot establish that first-step function necessarily requires sustained maintenance.

BoundaryEntirely a mathematical model; real wear, maintenance timing, and failure thresholds require independent measurement. No maintenance amount is prescribed on this basis.

Mathematical construction: the same two backup paths, but different independent and common-cause failureTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth probability models are entirely stipulated, with instantaneous switching and sufficient capacity; model B is independent only conditional on no common-cause event.

Assume function is achieved when at least one of two paths is available. In model A, each path fails independently with probability 0.1, so dual-failure probability is 0.01. In model B, a common event with probability 0.05 causes both paths to fail; absent that event, each path fails conditionally independently with probability 1/19. Each path's marginal failure probability is still 0.05+0.95/19=0.1, but dual-failure probability is 0.05+0.95×(1/19)²=1/19≈0.052632. The number of paths and individual marginal probabilities are identical, but system-failure probabilities differ. Counting backups cannot replace examination of shared conditions.

BoundaryThese are not reliability statistics for actual equipment; reality also requires switching time, authority, skills, and capacity.

Teaching construction: enough backup capacity can still miss the functional windowTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDeadlines, capacity, and switching rules are teaching assumptions, with no real shutdown or personnel experiment.

A fictional service allows at most 2 minutes of interruption. Its backup has sufficient capacity but requires on-site personnel to switch it over, taking at least 5 minutes. A backup's existence does not satisfy F of ‘interruption no longer than 2 minutes.’ Restoring service after 5 minutes is still another real result; the backup is not therefore entirely useless, nor can late recovery be written as meeting the original window.

BoundaryThis is not a real safety threshold or switching recommendation; task requirements must be fixed beforehand.

Mathematical construction: lower central workload may coincide with more external replacement workTeaching scenario

AssumptionsConstructed same-type labor time, covering both sides without double counting. Person-hours serve only as time accounting, without assuming equal fatigue, opportunity losses, or rights across people.

Suppose maintenance labor for the same activity on the list in the same week initially totals 8 person-hours centrally and 0 externally. After a change it totals 3 centrally and 7 externally. Central labor falls by 5 person-hours, but total labor under this accounting definition rises from 8 to 10 person-hours. External replacement work can explain maintained output; central work orders alone cannot establish reduced total maintenance.

BoundaryTime, health, risk, and responsibility are not combined into a universal cost; no real family or institution is described.

STS-114: spare parts must enter actual replacementDocumented case

NASA's mission record states that during the second extravehicular activity on August 1, 2005, Noguchi and Robinson removed failed CMG-1, moved a new control moment gyroscope out of the payload bay, and installed it. The record then reports four working CMGs on the space station. This section adds the distinction among a spare part's existence, transportation to position, personnel operations, installation, and operating state, rather than repeating the image-feedback case.

SourceNASA STS-114 mission page, updated 2025-05-01Mission Highlights, EVA No.2 (Aug.1) entry; for CMG function, see the sentence following the preceding EVA No.1 entryReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis supports the mission record of that replacement and the operating count at the time. It does not quantify long-term reliability, independent redundancy, or every counterfactual concerning maintenance necessity, and does not confer eligibility for a formal channel-effect test.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTwo backup units share the same power source and sole approver, yet are declared two fully independent recovery paths.

What it limitsCommon exposure and switching authority may block both simultaneously; test against failure conditions.

Teaching counterexampleAn old process retains its identity while its task function remains impaired, so continued maintenance of the old process is called repair.

What it limitsPreserving identity differs from meeting the functional target; mismatched maintenance may require stopping or transformation.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleSomeone continually fills gaps to keep a service normal, so they are presumed permanently obliged to continue.

What it limitsSeparate empirical uptake from normative obligation; check voluntariness, responsibility, and the right to stop.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleHaving purchased parts conforming to an interface standard, declaring that the on-site fault can immediately be solved.

What it limitsImplementation versions, semantics, environment, quality, arrival, skills, and shutdown authority may still be inadequate.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • No need for sustained maintenance in a short window does not imply no need in every longer window; long-window evidence also cannot replace the original short-task conclusion.
  • Current wear may sufficiently take up the past; a historical-increment test need not be required before recognizing cumulative carrier effects.
  • If one still says ‘maintaining the same object’ after the original identity criterion fails, check whether transformation or disintegration has occurred; do not silently retain the old definition.
  • Redundancy tests under normal power and transportation conditions do not automatically cover common-cause failures and recovery phases.
  • Improved central metrics may accompany increased external labor; maintenance capability does not directly create an obligation for any named person.

Scope and open questions

The real mission supplies specific replacement actions and operating states. Reliability, wear, switching, and external time accounting are explicit mathematical/teaching constructions, not presented as NASA data.

Why does the wear model with m=1 first fail at step four?

Wear proceeds through 1,2,3,4. F permits ≤3, so the threshold is first exceeded at step four.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why can model B's dual failure not be calculated as 0.1×0.1?

The two paths are conditionally independent only in the absence of the common event; overall, they are coupled by the common cause. First condition the probability calculation on that event.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If maintenance is necessary to preserve function, does that suffice to designate a particular employee to continue bearing it?

No. Maintenance mechanisms, responsibility, obligation, voluntariness, and authority are different judgments.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why might recovery targets remain unmet despite an existing backup with enough capacity?

There may be common failure, switching delays, gaps in on-site skills or authority, and recovery dependencies may be unavailable within the same window.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If current wear fully reflects the past and additional history provides no increment, does this exclude cumulative maintenance effects?

No. The carrier-cumulative route holds on separate longitudinal/causal evidence; only the additional historical branch requires a historical-increment test.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

6.6Load, Capacity, and Recovery (CM-LOAD) ​

In brief‘We cannot keep up’ and ‘recovery is complete’ both need explicit definitions. Where, during which period, for what demand, and with how much available capacity? Has the day's output recovered, identity and function, or depleted reserves? A single overall percentage cannot answer these questions.

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); channel effect (§4.4). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). Demand and capacity must be quantities of the same type or have explicit units and a conversion mapping. Demand, available capacity, replenishment, and spillover need to be measured in the same time window and at the same position. A channel-effect test supports only the measured channel and its relevant dimensions.

The mechanism chain is:

Demand of a matching type enters the specified channel → occupies available capacity → produces an immediate gap or cross-boundary spillover → load reduction/replenishment/capacity expansion changes the gap

To explain subsequent accumulation or delayed recovery, separately check the carriers of damage, capacity, or recovery and their effects across time windows.

The load mechanism has three branches. The instantaneous branch determines only the demand–capacity relation of the same type and the immediate gap within the same time window. The carrier-accumulation branch checks under §4.5 how historical exposure formed the current damage or capacity state, how that state is retained or recovers across time windows, and the subsequent outcomes and comparison conditions. A causal claim must have grounds for identification appropriate to the claim. The historical-increment branch is of the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test separately tests the conditional increment beyond the current representation. Capacity that expands at the same time can absorb demand. An instantaneous gap may leave no lasting difference once it closes. Load therefore need not accumulate monotonically, and an instantaneous overload need not cause damage or collapse.

Load must be stated by position and distribution. A mean alone is insufficient. For capacity, distinguish peak and sustained levels, alternative channels, and replenishment. For recovery, distinguish recovery of visible output, recovery of identity or function, and recovery of the internal margin. Quantities of different types cannot be directly subtracted. A need for recovery does not by itself impose a duty to make sacrifices on any subject or grant any subject authorization.

A recovery judgment should state at the same time what recovered, for whom, under what support conditions, and through what point in time. The following are evidenced separately: the quantity, quality, continuity, and accessibility of actual output; staff recuperation, spare parts, maintenance backlogs, and continuity of funding; the added burdens outside the boundary from care, commuting, borrowing money, or substitute services; and subsequent disruptions and near misses. The pre-disaster population, current population, eligible people, and actual users must not be silently substituted for one another when calculating recovery rates. Confirming that a particular limited function has recovered does not require all other outcomes to recover at the same time.

Temporary facilities, continuing outside support, or assistive equipment can provide real functional repair. Dependence on support does not by itself indicate failed recovery. The sustainability and expiration of support should be verified, along with whether alternative uptake is already in operation. Any demand peaks, maintenance cycles, or seasonal exposures that have yet to be experienced should also be stated. The term “false recovery” should be reserved for a claim that extends beyond what the evidence supports about the object, population, function, or conditions for continuation. That alone provides no basis for inferring deception. If destabilization recurs after recovery, several possibilities must be compared separately: the persistence of earlier damage, unreplenished reserves, interruption of support, new shocks, and changes in measurement definitions. A new failure must not erase an earlier result stated within its proper limits. Necessary support must not be withdrawn to validate recovery.

6.6Note

Understanding this section

6.6 Load, capacity, and recovery (CM-LOAD)

‘We cannot keep up’ and ‘recovery is complete’ both need explicit definitions. Where, during which period, for what demand, and with how much available capacity? Has the day's output recovered, identity and function, or depleted reserves? A single overall percentage cannot answer these questions.

The “Load, Capacity, and Recovery” mechanism first uses structural object (§3.1) to specify objects and locations, then a channel-effect test (§4.4) to identify measured channels and relevant dimensions; the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) are method requirements. Demand and capacity must be of the same type, or have explicit units and conversion mappings, measured at the same location and within the same window. Tasks per hour cannot directly be subtracted from total inventory, nor headcounts from budgets. Processing time, task types, accounting boundaries, and mappings must be provided before comparison becomes possible.

The mechanism chain is comparable demand entering a specified channel, occupying available capacity, and producing an immediate shortfall or cross-boundary spillover, followed by load reduction, replenishment, or expansion changing the shortfall. The instantaneous branch determines only demand-capacity and immediate shortfall within the same window; one shortfall does not automatically imply accumulated damage. The carrier-accumulation branch additionally traces historical exposure forming current damage/capacity carriers, retention or recovery across windows, subsequent outcomes, and proportionate causal comparisons; only the historical-increment branch separately adds a historical-increment test.

Load need not accumulate monotonically. Capacity may expand with demand and absorb the increment; a brief shortfall may end without persistent differences. Delayed recovery or later collapse requires explaining how damage, reserves, backlog, or another carrier connects one window to the next. “Was once overloaded” cannot be a sufficient cause of every later problem.

Averages cannot replace location and distribution. Total demand below total capacity does not ensure that every location avoids overload. Spare capacity that cannot reach the shortfall location within the window cannot directly offset it. Distinguish peak from sustained capacity, alternative-channel capacity, and replenishment rate; a brief peak cannot silently promise long-term supply. Register where cross-boundary spillover lands rather than deleting it from central indicators.

Recovery has at least three targets: whether output returns, whether the original identity or predefined function recovers, and whether internal margins are replenished. Normal output quantity may coexist with differences in quality, continuity, or accessibility. A restored function may coexist with unrestored staff rest, spare parts, maintenance backlog, or funding continuity. Conversely, confirming an accurately bounded function need not wait for every other life outcome to improve.

A recovery claim must specify what recovers, for whom, under which support, and through what date. Quantity, quality, continuity, and accessibility of physical or service outputs require separate evidence. Internal rest/spares/backlog/funding, external caregiving/commuting/borrowing/alternative-service burdens, and later interruptions and near misses cannot be inferred from central output alone. List unlike burdens separately; the need for recovery does not itself generate duties of sacrifice or operational authorization.

The denominator is part of the claim. Predisaster population, current population, eligible people, and actual users answer different questions, and the numerator must belong to the corresponding set. “100% service connection among those meeting safety conditions” can be true without meaning “100% recovery of all aspects of life for all predisaster residents.” Explain reasons, timing, and excluded positions when changing denominators; do not overwrite the old definition with the new.

Temporary premises, continued external aid, or assistive equipment can support genuine functional repair. Dependence on support is not failure; check how long support can last, its expiry, whether replacement uptake is actually operating, and peak loads, seasonal exposure, or maintenance cycles not yet experienced. Support does not mean recovery can never count, nor may supported success be generalized into independent success after withdrawal.

“False recovery” should identify only a claim exceeding evidence for objects, populations, functions, or persistence conditions, without thereby presuming deception. Later renewed instability requires comparing continuing old damage, unreplenished reserves, interrupted support, new shocks, and changed definitions. A new failure may reveal boundaries without erasing earlier accurately bounded achievements; necessary support must not be withdrawn to test recovery.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First declare object, location, population, time window, and demand/capacity types and units, supplying necessary conversion mappings.

  2. 2

    Measure actually available capacity, demand, replenishment, and spillover by location, distinguishing peak from sustained capability.

  3. 3

    State immediate, carrier-cumulative, and additional-historical-increment claims separately; the latter two require cross-window material, and the last separately requires a historical-increment test.

  4. 4

    Provide proportionate identification grounds for load reduction/replenishment/expansion effects, addressing common shocks and alternative channels.

  5. 5

    Recovery claims separately record output, identity or function, and internal reserves, listing quantity/quality/continuity/accessibility and internal/external burdens.

  6. 6

    Fix numerator and denominator; disclose support conditions, expiry, whether successor uptake is operating, and stress windows not yet experienced.

  7. 7

    For renewed instability, distinguish old damage, reserves, support, new shocks, and measurement changes; preserve bounded successes and separately review authority to act.

Distinctions to keep clear

Immediate shortfall

Demand exceeds available capacity at the same location and in the same window.

≠

Cumulative damage

Requires a carrier bringing past exposure forward; it does not follow directly from a shortfall.

Output recovery

A particular output, such as quantity, returns to a predefined level.

≠

Margin recovery

Restoring reserves, rest, backlog, and continuity capacity is another task.

Functional recovery under support

Temporary aid can form part of genuine function.

≠

Independent maintenance after support withdrawal

Requires proportionate later material; the former cannot substitute.

Bounded percentage

Explicit population, numerator and denominator, function, and time.

≠

Comprehensive recovery

Covers more objects and outcomes; one percentage does not automatically establish it.

Mathematical construction: overall surplus conceals local shortfallTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCapacity units are items/this hour and demand has a fixed task type; permission for intersite transfer is explicitly separated into two constructions.

At two fictional service points in the same hour, demands are 8 and 0 items and available capacities 5 and 5, for comparable tasks. Total demand 8 is below total capacity 10, but if transfer between sites is unavailable that hour, local shortfalls are max(0,8−5)=3 and 0, leaving 3 unfinished. An additional instantaneous, lossless, authorized dispatch channel could move those 3 tasks to the second site and clear this window's shortfall. That is an extra condition, not something totals automatically provide.

BoundaryNot actual organizational data; mathematical dispatchability does not imply real permission or lossless channels.

Mathematical construction: output returns before reservesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsStipulated damage-formation and recovery rules; output=min(demand,capacity), with no other shocks, inputs, or capacity adjustments.

A fictional system has rated capacity 5, with current damage z reducing available capacity to c=5−z; z stays between 0 and 5 throughout this example. Initially z₀=0. Round 0 demand is 7, giving shortfall g₀=max(0,7−5)=2. This round has no recovery, and the shortfall is written into damage, so z₁=2. Thereafter demand is 3 each round, shortfall max(0,3−c), and recovery is 1 unit through z_{t+1}=max(0,z_t+g_t−1). Round 1: c₁=3, output 3, z₂=1; round 2: c₂=4, output 3, z₃=0; round 3: c₃=5. Output already meets demand in round 1, but available capacity and margin have not returned to 5 and 2.

BoundaryReal overload need not produce this damage; the model establishes only that “output meets target” and “reserves restored” can occur at different times.

Mathematical construction: immediate shortfall need not leave damageTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExplicitly no backlog or persistent damage; unmet tasks still entail loss within that round and are not called impact-free.

Consider another fictional system with rated capacity 5, capacity fixed at 5 every round, and no retained damage. Demand is 7 in the first round and 3 in the second, giving outputs 5 and 3, with 2 unmet tasks in the first. If unfinished tasks terminate under an explicit rule instead of accumulating, the second round retains no state difference from that shortfall. The prior example's damage equation cannot be imposed merely because a shortfall of 2 occurred.

BoundaryDoes not apply to actual objects known to have backlog, persistent harm, or other carriers.

Mathematical construction: three true ratios answer different questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPure teaching numbers; connected accounts, actual use, and safety eligibility are different items. All 80 reconnected accounts are assumed to belong to both predisaster and current sets.

A fictional community had 100 predisaster accounts, now has 90, and 80 meet this round's safe-connection conditions and have all reconnected; there are 70 actual users. Assume the sets and times have been checked with no double counting. Eligible connection rate is 80/80=100%; the reconnected share of predisaster accounts is 80/100=80%; actual usage among current accounts is 70/90≈77.8%. Each numerator and denominator has its own meaning; 100% cannot be rewritten as restored use by every predisaster account.

BoundaryDoes not correspond to actual Puerto Rico population counts or evaluate power quality, continuity, or health outcomes.

Puerto Rico electricity restoration: denominators and temporary support jointly bound recoveryDocumented case

GAO's 2019 report relays PREPA's estimate that, by August 2018, all customers who could safely receive electricity had service restored. The report explicitly says this did not mean all predisaster customers, because some buildings were unsafe to reconnect. GAO also records that, as of December 11, 2018, USACE still supported 7 generators powering microgrids on Vieques and Culebra. This section focuses on recovery denominators and conditions of continued support: electricity service can genuinely recover without establishing full restoration of all old customers, original grid configurations, and long-term continuity.

SourceGAO-19-296，2019-04-18Printed pp.6–7: Status of electricity restoration and the temporary-generator passage after Figure 1; PDF pp.10–11Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe report itself openly limits its definition; it is not evidence of deception. Connection counts do not establish recovery of personal lives, health, or all reserves, and no judgment is made about the current grid.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAverage demand is below average capacity, so every location has no load problem.

What it limitsThis does not eliminate local overload or inability to dispatch resources.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleTemporary generation or continuing external aid remains, so local function never genuinely recovered.

What it limitsSupport can form genuine functional recovery; specify its conditions, continuity, and scope.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleA new shock causes another interruption, so all earlier records of supply recovery within a bounded period were false.

What it limitsDifferent windows and shocks require separate checks; do not erase accurate facts backward or directly presume deception.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleCentral output recovers, so staff rest, spare parts, maintenance backlog, and external caregiving burdens have all recovered.

What it limitsObtain separate evidence for output, internal/external reserves, and distribution.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Quantities of different types, times, or locations cannot be directly subtracted; dispatchability is also a bridging condition.
  • Brief overload may leave no long-term damage; long-term capacity shortage may also have other independent causes.
  • A bounded function holding does not mean every outcome has recovered, nor must every outcome recover before that function is acknowledged.
  • If support will expire without an operating successor, persistence remains unresolved; do not invent future supply.
  • Renewed instability does not automatically overturn earlier bounded success, establish deception by prior personnel, or require withdrawing support.

Scope and open questions

The official investigation directly distinguishes recovery denominators, support conditions, and continuity; local load, damage trajectories, and account ratios are separately labeled mathematical constructions, not disaster-area data.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why can 3 tasks remain unfinished when capacities at two sites total 10 and demand totals 8?

  2. 2

    In the damage example, why does output 3 meeting demand in round 1 not establish margin recovery?

  3. 3

    If function meets its target with assistive equipment, must the equipment first be removed for recovery to count as real?

  4. 4

    Does a 100% connection rate among eligible people imply 100% among predisaster accounts?

  5. 5

    Which explanations should be compared for renewed instability?

Why can 3 tasks remain unfinished when capacities at two sites total 10 and demand totals 8?

Demand is concentrated at the first site with capacity 5, and dispatch is unavailable in this window; its local shortfall is not automatically offset by spare capacity at the second site.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

In the damage example, why does output 3 meeting demand in round 1 not establish margin recovery?

Capacity was only 3 against demand 3, leaving margin 0; the margin of 2 for the same demand at rated capacity 5 had not returned.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If function meets its target with assistive equipment, must the equipment first be removed for recovery to count as real?

No. Recovery may already hold under the original support conditions. Independent maintenance after withdrawal is a separate claim; necessary support must not be removed merely for validation.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does a 100% connection rate among eligible people imply 100% among predisaster accounts?

No: the denominators differ. In the construction the former is 80/80, the latter 80/100.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Which explanations should be compared for renewed instability?

Continuing old damage, unreplenished reserves, support interruption, new shocks, and changed measurement definitions, checking the timing and carriers for each.

6.7Phase and Threshold Transition (CM-PHASE) ​

In briefA system may operate differently in different ranges, but a kinked curve alone does not show that a particular cause triggered it, still less an inevitable upgrade. First confirm that it remains the same object, then distinguish the evidence required for patterns, triggers, persistence, and history.

Basic grounds: structural object (§3.1); basic state terms (§3.2). The epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4) and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) are the shared method requirements for the phase-pattern branch. Add the conditions for causal claims (§2.4) when making a causal claim about a trigger, persistence through a carrier, or historical-increment hysteresis. They are not a prerequisite for basic pattern classification, and a purely predictive historical increment does not thereby become causal. Basic phase identification does not require a historical-increment test. Under the same definition of the candidate object and the same identity criterion, it is possible to test whether there are at least two reproducibly distinguishable ranges of operation once the state variables, candidate parameters or trigger conditions, threshold, and robustness to noise and binning have been stated in advance.

The mechanism judgments have the following branches.

The phase-pattern branch. It requires “the same identity criterion, two reviewable intervals, and a threshold pattern fixed in advance.” It determines only the relation between the intervals and the threshold and makes no causal claim about the trigger.

The causal-triggering branch. It requires “a specified trigger channel and either an intervention on the channel or natural variation suitable for identification.” A channel-effect test is also required to locate the effect of the trigger.

The carrier-persistence branch checks how, under the same identity criterion, the current carrier maintains a phase, sustains it across time windows, or gives rise to delayed recovery. Use §4.5 to document the carrier and temporal order, make longitudinal comparisons, and obtain causal evidence appropriate to the claim. The hysteresis branch of the “Phase and Threshold Transition” mechanism is limited to the historical-increment kind. A historical-increment test separately tests the conditional increment beyond the current representation. An identical curve shape cannot stand in for evidence under any route.

The phase conclusion should be withdrawn in three cases: a continuous trend already fully explains the change within the same state distribution; the threshold shifts arbitrarily with the way of binning; or the identity criterion had already ceased to hold before the transition. These are recorded instead as continuous change, an effect of how the measurements were partitioned, and object conversion or dissolution, respectively. A reversible phase need not have a historical path. Only the historical-increment hysteresis branch adds a historical-increment test. Phases do not form a mandatory sequence of maturation through the seven state prototypes (§8.3). A new phase does not thereby rank higher, become better, or carry greater authorization.

6.7Note

Understanding this section

6.7 Phase and threshold transition (CM-PHASE)

A system may operate differently in different ranges, but a kinked curve alone does not show that a particular cause triggered it, still less an inevitable upgrade. First confirm that it remains the same object, then distinguish the evidence required for patterns, triggers, persistence, and history.

The basic grounds are structural object (§3.1) and basic state terms (§3.2). Fix the definition of the same candidate object and its identity criterion, state in advance the state variables, candidate parameters or triggering conditions, and thresholds, and check robustness to noise and binning before testing at least two reproducibly distinguishable operating ranges. “The same identity criterion” means more than unchanged wording: the object must continue to satisfy that identity criterion across the compared ranges. If the old identity criterion has failed, phase terminology cannot conceal object change.

The phase-pattern branch determines only a range–threshold pattern. Its shared method requirements are the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4) and the conditions for evidence (§2.5), requiring treatment of continuous trends, noise, measurement classification, and other competing explanations, but not causal identification as a prerequisite for every pattern classification. Reproducibly observing different ranges does not establish what caused the transition.

Only the causal-triggering branch requires a specified triggering channel, channel intervention or natural variation with identification conditions, and a separate channel-effect test locating the triggering effect, adding the responsibilities set by the conditions for causal claims (§2.4). Temporal sequence, changes near a threshold, or predictive accuracy alone cannot eliminate common inputs, reverse effects, or selection; causal claims carry additional material responsibilities beyond determining a pattern.

The carrier-persistence branch explains how a current carrier maintains a phase, persistence across windows, or delayed recovery under the same identity criterion, requiring carrier, timing, longitudinal comparison, and proportionate causal evidence. In this book the hysteresis branch specifically means historical-increment hysteresis: history still supplies conditional increment relative to an explicit current representation, separately requiring a historical-increment test. A hysteresis loop in a domain may have its own physical or empirical explanation, but its looped shape alone cannot retrospectively award eligibility for this branch.

If the current carrier already records states determining what follows, the current state may fully take up path effects and additional historical increment may disappear. Basic reversible phases need no historical path at all. A predictive historical comparison does not automatically become historical causation because it is called “hysteresis”; causal triggering, carrier-persistence mechanisms, and historical causal explanations each add proportionate conditions for causal claims.

Three contrary situations require different records: if a continuous trend within one state distribution already suffices, discard unnecessary phase partitioning; if thresholds shift with arbitrary binning, prioritize measurement-classification effects; if the identity criterion fails before transition, examine object conversion, dissolution, or reclassification. A further formal object-conversion claim still follows its corresponding mapping and the conditions of a scale-closure test (§4.6); changing the wording of the identity criterion cannot automatically certify it.

Robustness does not require every threshold to be identical; it requires specifying in advance the noise ranges, binning choices, and observation windows under which results remain reviewable. Where classification near boundaries is unreliable, retain transition/unresolved regions rather than deleting inconvenient points afterward. Repeated appearance of a region also does not automatically make it an irreversible stage of maturity.

Phases in this section are not a mandatory sequence through the seven state prototypes (§8.3). A new phase need not be more efficient, more normatively justified, or more authorized; reversal is not automatically regression. Comparing merits, bearing costs, and implementing interventions still require predetermined tasks, norms, and authority, not a direction on a graph.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix the complete definition of the object and its identity criterion, checking that comparison regions continue to satisfy identity; do not change the criterion afterward to preserve the conclusion.

  2. 2

    Specify the states, parameters, thresholds, noise tolerances, and binning tests in advance, first judging the reproducible pattern.

  3. 3

    A pattern reports only relationships between regions; a claim about triggering causes additionally requires a channel-effect test for the specified channel and proportionate causal identification.

  4. 4

    To claim persistence or delayed recovery, locate the current carrier and its cross-window effects; to additionally claim a historical increment, run a historical-increment test.

  5. 5

    Separate predictive historical gains from historical causation; curve shape does not replace branch materials.

  6. 6

    Reclassify continuous trends, binning effects, and failure of the identity criterion into their appropriate results; formal conversion claims require a separate check of their conditions.

  7. 7

    Preserve the respective scopes of patterns, mechanisms, task merit, and action authorization; do not draw an automatic staircase of maturity.

Distinctions to keep clear

Phase pattern

A repeatably distinguishable region–threshold relationship within the same object.

≠

Triggering causation

A change in a specified channel causes a transition between regions; additional identification is required.

Carrier persistence

The current internal state takes up the past and maintains the phase.

≠

Additional historical hysteresis

An increment exists beyond the explicit current representation, additionally requiring a historical-increment test.

A loop in a physical curve

May suggest path or state memory, but the model and measurements must be checked.

≠

Historical-increment qualification

Cannot be determined solely by shape and is not automatically causal.

Different regions of the same object

The object continues to satisfy the original identity criterion.

≠

Object conversion/dissolution

The original identity criterion fails or the definition changes; judge separately.

Mathematical construction: two reversible regions without historical memoryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA deterministic state rule with bounded measurement error; p is measured exactly, threshold 2 and the noise bound are specified before calculation, and the identity criterion does not change with x being 0 or 1.

A fictional control unit continues to satisfy a predetermined identity criterion, with input p∈[0,4] and state rule x=0 when p<2 and x=1 when p≥2; measurement is y=x+ε, with |ε|≤0.1. The two output intervals are [-0.1,0.1] and [0.9,1.1], distinguishable by any classification boundary h∈(0.1,0.9). Inputs 1.5→2.5→1.5 give states 0→1→0, depending only on current p without retaining history. The rule is stipulated within the model, showing that a pattern and reversibility can exist without additional history.

BoundaryThe two regions are mathematical stipulations rather than actual repeated measurements; real-world phase-pattern or causal-trigger qualification still requires its own materials.

Mathematical construction: binning can create a false impression of a jumpTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe continuous function is completely known, and the label rule is the analyst's artificial binning; there are no actual observational data.

Let the underlying model instead be y=p, with p varying continuously over [0,4] and no state jump. The reporter publishes only labels L=0 when y<2 and L=1 when y≥2, making the plotted label jump abruptly. Changing the bin boundary to 3 moves the label's jump to 3, while the original y=p remains unchanged. A classification threshold moving with reporting rules is insufficient to establish a phase conversion of the object.

BoundaryThis does not deny that discrete classifications can be useful; it shows only that classification use and identification of object phases are different.

Mathematical construction: a current carrier can sufficiently take up a hysteresis loopTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe rule and initial endpoints are artificially given, with no other noise or hidden states; s must be disclosed, not deleted to manufacture historical gains.

Let state s∈{0,1}, with rule s′=1 when p≥2, s′=0 when p≤1, and s′=s when 1<p<2; output is s′. Path A enters 1.5 from p=0.5, with current s=0; path B enters 1.5 from p=2.5, with current s=1. The same p=1.5 can yield different outputs, but the complete current representation (p,s) already determines the next step; recording only p omits the known carrier s. This model with memory explains why a hysteresis shape does not automatically require additional history beyond the complete current representation.

BoundaryMathematical carrier sufficiency does not deny real-world historical increments; actual comparisons still collect evidence according to the selected representation and the conditions of a historical-increment test.

Teaching construction: identity criteria determine the question's boundariesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe objects and criteria are teaching constructions; no identity criterion is claimed to be the uniquely natural boundary.

For a fictional lamp, if the predetermined identity criterion requires that the same numbered housing and wiring components still constitute the apparatus, on/off can be states within the same object. If a different task takes ‘this particular burning flame’ as its candidate object, its identity criterion may cease to hold when the flame goes out; a newly lit flame cannot universally be called the original object changing phase. The specific identity criterion must be stated with the task in advance, rather than chosen freely after observing results.

BoundaryDefining criteria only declares candidates; it does not establish empirical object validity or formal conversion.

NIST's triple-point cell: first distinguish physical phases from object boundariesDocumented case

NIST's triple-point cell description, published on December 21, 2016, describes a sealed glass container holding water of a specified isotopic composition and a state of equilibrium among solid, liquid, and vapor phases inside the cell. For this section, ‘this sealed container and its contents’ can explicitly be selected as the candidate object before studying its internal phases. This object delineation is the analyst's declaration; the appearance of different internal states of matter cannot automatically be written as replacement of the container object.

Scope and limitsThe source supports a phase-state description of an actual metrological apparatus; it supplies neither complete pre-registered threshold/noise tests under this framework nor evidence that any organization has the same phases or a maturity sequence.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleFirst divide a continuous score into two groups using an arbitrary threshold, then use the two groups to prove natural phases.

What it limitsThe classification rule itself cannot serve as independent evidence of an object's regional pattern.

Teaching counterexampleObserve a hysteresis loop and declare historical-increment causation established without measuring the current carrier.

What it limitsCurve shape cannot replace carrier control, a historical-increment test, and proportionate causal grounds.

Teaching counterexampleThe original object's identity has already failed, yet it is still described as the same object entering a more mature phase.

What it limitsThis exceeds both object boundaries and the bounds of value upgrading; check conversion/dissolution and evaluate objectives separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The basic pattern has no hard requirement for a historical-increment test or every causal requirement; an appropriate pattern description may be retained without identifying a trigger.
  • Repeated regions cannot be artificially manufactured through arbitrary binning; known continuous relationships must be included as competing explanations.
  • When the current state is already sufficient, zero additional history does not cancel carrier persistence or reversible phases.
  • The identity criterion cannot be rewritten after results to obtain a phase conclusion; identity must be checked against the original task and materials.
  • Physical phases in nature and operating regions in social systems have no automatic equivalence or stage mapping.

Scope and open questions

The official metrological apparatus description supplies concrete physical phases and boundary identification; proofs concerning reversibility, binning, and hysteresis use separate mathematical models with complete assumptions, without substituting physical analogy for social evidence.

If a pattern recurs but the triggering channel has not been identified, must the entire pattern description be deleted?

No. Record the regional relationships in a bounded way under the pattern branch; record triggering causation separately as unresolved.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why can h=0.5 distinguish noisy states in the first construction?

The low interval's maximum is 0.1 and the high interval's minimum is 0.9; 0.5 lies in the gap. Any h in (0.1,0.9) works.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

In the hysteresis model, can the next step be uniquely calculated given p=1.5 but unknown s? What if (p,s) is given?

Knowing only p is insufficient, since s may be 0 or 1; knowing complete (p,s) gives s′=s, so the current carrier determines the future.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does every phase study require the conditions for causal claims as a basic requirement?

No. The pattern branch's common method requirements are “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” and the conditions for evidence; claims of causal triggering, carrier-persistence mechanisms, or historical causal explanations add proportionate causal responsibilities.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why does the appearance of a new phase not directly mean improvement?

A phase only classifies operating regions; task benefits, costs, norms, and authority require separate judgments.

6.8Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction (CM-SELECTION) ​

In briefSeeing a practice or type persist makes it tempting to reason backward that ‘it must be better’. This section first sets aside judgments of merit to examine what variations exist, how outcomes differ, whether the differences actually enter the next round, and whether sampling luck alone is sufficient to explain them.

Basic grounds: basic state terms (§3.2). Must also meet three method requirements: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5). This mechanism is set out on its own as conditions that can be tested. It does not follow automatically from the definition of “evolution has occurred,” and a conceptual explanation or the framework’s own account cannot establish it directly.

The three outputs must be kept separate.

The selection pattern. It requires “variation, difference, retention, entry into the next round, repeated rounds, and random drift as a competing explanation.” Before the results are seen, define distinguishable variations (written V) and their sources. In comparable environments, observe differential outcomes (written D) that exceed the threshold. The differences carry forward into the next round through retention (written R) and can be reviewed across repeated rounds. Test random drift, common external causes, and sampling bias at the same time. Its basic grounds are the basic state terms alone.

The specific mechanism. It requires “a specified channel of retention or reproduction and either a perturbation of the channel or natural variation suitable for identification.” Beyond an established selection pattern, a channel-effect test is also required to locate the mechanism that carries the process.

The path across rounds. It requires “a conditional increment from historical terms across rounds and control for the current state.” Beyond an established selection pattern, a historical-increment test is also required.

Change without a differential outcome amounts to change alone. A one-off difference with no retention, no entry into the next round, and no repeated rounds is a one-off outcome. If the random-drift model is already sufficient, no selection pattern is determined. If retention remains unchanged after the candidate reproduction channel is perturbed, that specific mechanism is not determined. A single case of persistence does not amount to differential retention. What is retained does not thereby become better, more advanced, or more justified. Systemic selection is distinct from choice by an acting subject, and still more from collective governance choice (§14.2). A choice by an acting subject requires a subject, options, and evidence of a decision. Collective governance choice requires normative premises, authorization within the scope of authorization, and operational procedures.

6.8Note

Understanding this section

6.8 Variation–differential retention–reproduction (CM-SELECTION)

Seeing a practice or type persist makes it tempting to reason backward that ‘it must be better’. This section first sets aside judgments of merit to examine what variations exist, how outcomes differ, whether the differences actually enter the next round, and whether sampling luck alone is sufficient to explain them.

Basic state terms (§3.2) only provide rules for using state terms such as change and evolution; ‘evolution occurred’ cannot directly imply selection. The “Variation–Differential Retention–Reproduction” mechanism is a separately operationalized conditional mechanism: the epistemic constraint “Retaining Competing Explanations and Residuals” (§4.8.4), the conditions for causal claims (§2.4), and the conditions for evidence (§2.5) handle competing explanations, causation, and material review, while conceptual stories do not generate empirical support. The basic pattern has no hard dependency on a channel-effect test or a historical-increment test, but still requires complete checks of V, D, R, the next round, repeated rounds, and competition with drift explanations.

V consists of distinguishable variations and their sources defined before outcomes; one cannot identify winners first and then treat their shared features as prior variables. D is a differential outcome exceeding a predetermined threshold in comparable environments, with proportionate denominators, exposures, and opportunity conditions; increased population size is not directly equivalent to improved per-unit retention or reproductive capacity. R is the retention that carries this difference into the next round, with repeated rounds available for review, not merely a statistical difference in the current round.

The pattern branch determines a selection pattern with these connections and must compare drift, common external causes, and sampling bias. Random sampling can also produce long-term dominance of a type, and failure to observe another type in a sample may simply reflect missed sampling. If a drift model explains the observations under proportionate sufficiency conditions, do not determine a selection pattern beyond it; mere nonsignificance likewise does not establish drift sufficiency, so retain judgment precision and failure records.

Beyond the pattern, the specific-mechanism branch identifies which retention or reproduction channel carries the difference, locating it through channel perturbation or natural variation satisfying identification conditions and a channel-effect test. If perturbing the candidate channel leaves retention unchanged, it cannot continue to be treated as the claimed specific mechanism; also check whether the perturbation actually took effect, alternative paths, and measurement conditions. Lack of support for a specified channel does not automatically cancel a pattern supported by other materials.

Beyond the pattern, the cross-round path branch separately tests conditional increments of cross-round historical terms after controlling for the current state, supported by a historical-increment test. Repeated rounds are a basic-pattern requirement; an additional historical increment is another requirement. Recurrence does not imply that history remains additionally useful given the complete current state. Conversely, a predictive historical variable alone does not establish V/D/R or selection channels.

When items are missing, stop at the appropriate level: with change but no D, record change; with only one difference but no R, next round, or replication, record a one-time outcome; if drift is sufficient, do not add a selection explanation; if a specified reproductive mechanism has not been distinguished, retain the pattern or candidate without inventing a channel. Results departing from expectations do not permit changing V, thresholds, environments, or historical controls afterward to rescue the original claim.

Being retained does not mean being more advanced, more normatively justified, or even better in every environment and task. A type replicating more under particular conditions is only a bounded process result; environmental changes, tradeoffs, frequency dependence, and coexistence can all limit narratives of ‘winning forever’.

System selection, an agent's choice, and collective governance choices are three different matters. System selection may have no unified decision-maker; agent choice requires a specific agent, options, and decision evidence; collective governance additionally requires normative premises, authorization within the scope of authorization, and operational procedures. ‘The mechanism retained this institution’ cannot decide public consent on people's behalf or authorize eliminating people and allocating resources.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Before results, define variations and sources, comparable environments, differential outcomes, thresholds, and next-round units.

  2. 2

    Separately check D's denominators and opportunity conditions, R's retention connections, and multiple subsequent rounds.

  3. 3

    Make proportionate comparisons with drift, common external causes, and sampling bias; do not rely solely on a one-time advantage or long-term existence.

  4. 4

    Report the pattern level first; a specified retention/reproduction mechanism additionally requires channel identification and a channel-effect test. Do not treat names as causation.

  5. 5

    For additional cross-round history, separately control the current state and run a historical-increment test; do not treat repetition itself as a historical conditional increment.

  6. 6

    When items are missing, narrow the result to change, a one-time outcome, a pattern, or an unresolved result; explicitly preserve every failure condition.

  7. 7

    Moving from process support to values, agent intentions, and governance authority always requires separate bridging materials; no automatic upgrading.

Distinctions to keep clear

Change/evolution

A change in a selected state variable or in an item of the object's definition.

≠

Selection pattern

Requires V/D/R, the next round, repetition, and competition with drift explanations.

One-time outcome difference

Different types have different outcomes in this round.

≠

Differential retention

The difference actually enters subsequent rounds and can be reviewed.

Selection pattern

A structure of differential retention under bounded conditions.

≠

Specific mechanism

Separately identify the specified carrier/reproduction channel.

System retention

A process causes some types to continue or increase.

≠

Governance decision

Requires agents, options, norms, authorization, and procedures.

Mathematical construction: how differential replication enters the next roundTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA fully specified nonbiological marker-copying model, with no actual experiment; deterministic rules exclude random drift by assumption rather than testing it away with data.

Take fictional marker types A/B, initially 4 each. Each round, each A marker produces 2 same-type successors and each B produces 1, under one rule with no capacity limits, mutation, or random sampling. Round one gives A=8,B=4, with A proportion 2/3; round two gives A=16,B=4, proportion 4/5. Generally, for current proportion p∈(0,1), p′=2p/(1+p), and p′−p=p(1−p)/(1+p)>0. V is the two types defined beforehand, D is their per-unit copy counts 2 and 1, R is retention in same-type successors, and repeated rounds follow the same recurrence.

BoundaryProves only differential retention in the specified model, not a real mechanism, indefinitely available resources, or any value superiority of A.

Mathematical construction: a one-round difference without retention across roundsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe reset rule is explicit; the unit of analysis is a complete round and the start of its successor. Numbers are constructed.

Keep the model, but after each round an external rule discards every successor and reinstates 4 A and 4 B. The intermediate 8-to-4 difference remains visible each round, but never enters the next round’s initial state; starting proportions stay at 1/2. If the predetermined question concerns frequency evolution across rounds, intermediate outcomes cannot stand for a completed R chain.

BoundaryA different question about within-round copying differences can retain the corresponding conclusion; failure across rounds does not deny every local fact.

Mathematical construction: pure drift can also fix rapidlyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsSampling rules and no mutation are mathematical assumptions, with equiprobable parents; no actual sampling occurred.

Take a fictional population containing one A and one B. Each generation independently samples twice with replacement, equally likely from either parent marker, copying their types into a next generation still of size 2. The types have no capability difference. The probability that the next generation is all A is (1/2)²=1/4; once all A, absence of mutation keeps it all A. Thus persistent all-A fixation may result from pure sampling rather than a higher per-unit reproduction rate for A.

Boundary‘Drift is also possible’ does not directly reject all actual selection; reality requires probability comparisons, repeated material, and predetermined criteria.

Mathematical construction: repeated selection needs no additional historyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe current representation contains every state and rule needed in this example, hiding no further differences.

In the first construction, current p and the fixed copying rule uniquely determine p′=2p/(1+p). Any two histories reaching the same p yield the same next proportion; history can explain how current p arose but adds nothing to this predetermined next-step prediction. Unrecorded heritable differences, environments, or carriers in reality prevent direct reuse of this sufficiency result.

BoundaryThe model’s zero additional increment is not evidence for a null conclusion in a real historical-increment test.

Coexistence in the long-term evolution experiment: selection need not leave only one winnerDocumented case

In their original 2008 study, Blount, Borland, and Lenski report in the results section on frequency-dependent selection that, after combining Cit− and Cit+ types at different initial proportions, both coexisted over subsequent rounds; Cit− approached a minority share rather than being completely eliminated by Cit+. The authors interpreted this result as negative frequency-dependent selection maintaining diversity. This section focuses on evidence containing types, trajectories across rounds, and competitive conditions, rather than merely on who remained at the end.

SourceBlount and colleagues, PNAS 105(23):7899–7906, issue dated 2008-06-10Results: ‘Frequency-Dependent Selection Maintains Ecological Diversity’, first two paragraphs; Methods: ‘Test for Frequency-Dependent Interaction’Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsRetain the ecological conclusion under the original study's bounded conditions; do not retrospectively grant the paper the status of a formal channel-effect test or historical-increment test under this framework, extrapolate to every environment, or call retained types more advanced or more normatively justified.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleSeeing one type persist for a long time is taken to imply necessarily superior differential-retention capability.

What it limitsEquiprobable drift can produce persistent fixation; other explanations still need comparison.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Empirical counterevidenceIn the relevant ecological comparison in Blount et al.’s 2008 study, Cit+ did not fix; Cit− remained a minority and coexisted with it.

What it limitsThis limits the universal claim that a new advantageous type necessarily eliminates all others; advantage and retention depend on specific environments and frequencies.

Blount et al.: historical contingency and innovation in long-term experimental populations

Teaching counterexampleAn institution survived prolonged competition, so everyone chose and consented to it and ought to obey it.

What it limitsSystem retention cannot establish agents’ decisions, public consent, or governance authorization.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleOne difference without subsequent tracking is declared an identified cross-round pathway mechanism.

What it limitsR, the next round, repetition, and current-state controls require distinct missing material; stop at the single outcome.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Random drift may produce persistent dominance; long-term existence is no shortcut to ruling out drift.
  • When the current state sufficiently determines what follows, repeated selection can occur without an additional historical increment.
  • Differential reproduction can occur alongside coexistence and need not cause other types to disappear.
  • When perturbing a channel fails to produce the expected effect, limit the conclusion to that channel and comparison conditions rather than generalizing to the impossibility of all selection.
  • A process advantage is not moral superiority, permission to act, or anyone's obligation to sacrifice.

Scope and open questions

The primary study specifically reports coexistence across rounds and the authors’ frequency-dependence interpretation, limiting one-round winner stories; mathematical marker examples are separate from the original study’s data and supply no experimental procedure.

What is A's share in the third round of the first construction?

A=32,B=4, proportion 32/36=8/9; alternatively substitute p=4/5 into 2p/(1+p).

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If the ratio resets to 4 to 4 at each round's end, why can the intermediate 8 to 4 not count as cross-round retention?

The intermediate difference is reset and never enters the next starting state; specify the round boundaries relevant to the task.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

In the pure-drift example, the probability of an all-A next generation is 1/4. What does this show, and what does it not show?

It shows that lasting advantage does not logically entail capability differences; it cannot establish that all actual advantages arise from drift.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If the pattern has been observed but channel perturbation does not show the expected change, may the pattern be retained?

Retain the pattern on its independent material while marking the specific channel mechanism unsupported or unresolved, checking perturbation implementation and alternative paths.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does repeated differential retention automatically satisfy a historical-increment test?

Not automatically. A historical-increment test asks whether history adds a conditional increment after controlling for explicitly specified current states.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above
