6.9Conditions for Coevolution ​

In briefTwo people, institutions, or species changing together need not be shaping each other. Coevolution requires checking how each direction acts separately; even if both ultimately return to the same point, their speed, risks, and intervention points along the way may differ completely.

A candidate for coevolution may be proposed when two candidate objects change each other’s environments, feasible paths, specified channels, or retention conditions and the effects in both directions are traceable within their respective time windows. The following must be stated separately: each object’s definition and identity criterion, their respective scales and time windows, the channel in each direction identified by a channel-effect test, temporal order, differences in speed, and the shared environment outside the two objects. Obtain separate evidence under §4.5 for carrier effects across rounds. Add the corresponding historical-increment tests separately only for claims of historical conditional increments beyond the current representation.

Joint change, synchronized fluctuations, and long-term correlation cannot substitute for bidirectional mechanisms. One-way dependence, common shocks, and synchronization of measurement protocols are all necessary competing explanations. Coevolution does not imply symmetry, mutual benefit, shared values, or a duty to maintain the relationship.

A shared final state does not establish a shared mechanism. Two processes can converge on the same fixed point while having different update rules, speeds of return, transients, and responses to intervention. A simpler representation may suffice if the only question concerns the long-run terminal value. The original conclusion does not automatically extend to questions about whether the target can be reached by a deadline or about targeted operations. Analyses of recovery, coevolution, and cross-circle continuation must retain these differences as required by the question. Converging curves are not taken as a substitute for identifying the mechanism.

6.9Note

Understanding this section

6.9 Conditions for Coevolution

Two people, institutions, or species changing together need not be shaping each other. Coevolution requires checking how each direction acts separately; even if both ultimately return to the same point, their speed, risks, and intervention points along the way may differ completely.

A coevolution candidate requires two candidate objects to change one another’s environments, feasible paths, specified channels, or retention conditions, with both directions traceable in their respective windows. ‘Co-’ refers to an interaction structure, not two rising curves, and guarantees no mutual benefit.

State separately two complete object definitions (§3.1), each with its own identity criterion, scale, and time window. One overall system name cannot replace the two objects, and the identity criterion cannot be called the whole definition of the object. They may have different time resolutions, update cycles, and visible ranges; align event timing and explain when A’s change to B might return to affect A, avoiding a synchronous mechanism invented from surface correlations between daily and annual data.

The channel-effect tests (§4.4) for the two directions carry separate identification responsibilities. Support for A→B does not establish B→A; one intervention changing both simultaneously may not distinguish directions either. Record transmitted content, effect locations, temporal order, comparison conditions, and speed differences, and proportionately test common third-party environmental changes, one-way dependence, and synchronized measurement protocols.

For cross-round effects, follow 4.5 to examine both sides’ current carriers, retention/updating, actual invocation, and longitudinal comparisons separately. Add the corresponding historical-increment tests only for a further claim of historical conditional increment beyond the current representation. Increment in one direction does not automatically establish increment in the other; persistent carriers on both sides also need not yield extra historical gains on both sides.

Coevolution need not be symmetric. Transmission strength, speed, costs, dependence, and ability to exit can differ greatly; the relation may be antagonistic rather than mutually beneficial. Even established two-way influence does not directly imply aligned values, public consent, an obligation to continue the relationship, or either party’s authority to act upon the other.

The same final state is not the same mechanism. A fixed point remains unchanged after updating; its existence alone does not guarantee trajectory convergence. Only separate proof of convergence permits discussing a trajectory’s long-term limit; update rules also determine return speed, transient peaks, and intervention responses. A simpler representation may suffice if the task asks only for a long-term limit under certain conditions. Once it asks about meeting a threshold within two steps, peaks, whom to change selectively, or performance after support removal, relevant distinctions must be retained and tested again.

Recovery, coevolution, and cross-circle continuity can all share terminal values while differing in process. Two curves eventually approaching each other cannot identify two-way channels; nor can an accurate original long-term summary handle new action tasks automatically. Preserve the scope of ‘which representation suffices for which target, horizon, and operation’ so model simplification is not mistaken for the world’s only mechanism.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Declare complete object definitions for A and B separately, with identity criteria, scale profiles, and time windows, ensuring each remains independently traceable.

  2. 2

    Specify A→B and B→A channels and the changed items separately, with timing, speed, and comparisons.

  3. 3

    Check the channel effects in the two directions separately, distinguishing shared environments, one-way dependence, and synchronized measurement protocols.

  4. 4

    For cross-round claims, first examine each carrier route; declare and test additional historical increments separately rather than passing them together.

  5. 5

    Treat long-term limits, arrival deadlines, transients, and targeted interventions as different tasks, checking representational preservation for each.

  6. 6

    Allow asymmetric or antagonistic coevolution to be reported; values, obligations to continue, and authority require separate consideration.

Distinctions to keep clear

Joint change

Both sides change during the same period.

≠

Two-way effects

Both causal paths have separate material; correlation cannot substitute.

Interaction

Each side can affect the other.

≠

Symmetry or mutual benefit

Magnitudes, speeds, gains, and burdens still require separate measurements.

The same fixed point

Two rules share a state unchanged by updating; a common long-term limit requires separate proof of convergence.

≠

The same dynamics and intervention mechanism

Identical updates, transients, and operation responses: a stronger, different claim.

Carriers across rounds

Current states preserve the past and affect what follows.

≠

Additional historical increment

History still adds gain given the current representation; check each direction separately.

Mathematical construction: the same endpoint, different speed and intervention responseTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFully specified fixed linear two-state models without external shocks or execution limits; r is the corresponding row-sum bound, and variables are deviations rather than headcounts.

Let two state deviations be z=(x,y). Model A updates x′=0.25x+0.25y, y′=0.25x+0.25y; model B updates x′=0.75x+0.125y, y′=0.125x+0.75y. Maximum row sums are 0.5 and 0.875 respectively, so for every finite initial state ||z_t||∞≤r^t||z₀||∞→0, and both have unique fixed point (0,0). Starting at (1,0), however, A gives (0.25,0.25) after one step and (0.125,0.125) after two; B gives (0.75,0.125) and then (0.578125,0.1875). If the task requires second-step maximum absolute deviation ≤0.2, A passes and B fails. If current y alone increases by δ while x stays fixed, next-step x changes by 0.25δ and 0.125δ respectively, so targeted intervention responses differ too.

BoundaryThis construction proves that terminal values cannot recover a mechanism; it does not independently establish coevolution of real objects or supply an actual intervention proposal.

Mathematical construction: shared input can synchronize two curves perfectlyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn explicit shared-input structure with no hidden cross-terms; all sequences are constructed.

Let external condition U_t vary arbitrarily, with x_t=U_t and y_t=2U_t and no links between them. They synchronize perfectly and may be highly correlated; yet replacing y alone while keeping U and the other rule fixed does not change later x. Testing a two-way relation requires asking separately whether change in each direction is caused by input from the other, rather than omitting the shared U.

BoundaryA shared environment and two-way relations can coexist in reality; naming a shared input does not automatically negate coevolution.

Teaching construction: one contemporaneous table cannot replace two clocksTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPurely a teaching timeline with no institution observed; update cycles are declared beforehand.

Fictional A adjusts its supply interface weekly, while B revises its usage rules quarterly. A’s change this week need not appear in B’s report that same week; B’s change next quarter may also arise from other conditions. State separately when supply actually changes B’s feasible paths and when B’s rules return to affect A, then compare within their respective windows. Copying quarterly totals into weekly rows cannot create more independent evidence merely through more table rows.

BoundaryNeither deny delayed effects from short-run nonsynchrony nor attribute every later change to the earliest A.

Bacteria and bacteriophages: coevolution can be antagonisticDocumented case

The public abstract of Buckling and Rainey’s 2002 original paper reports sustained reciprocal adaptation in bacterial-host resistance and phage infectivity: hosts developed resistance to a broader range of parasite types, while parasites gained infectivity against a broader range of host types. Replicate communities also diverged in their paths of change. This case directly limits the interpretation that coevolution equals mutually beneficial synchrony.

SourceBuckling & Rainey 2002，DOI 10.1098/rspb.2001.1945Original paper’s public Abstract, paragraphs two and three; Proc. R. Soc. B 269:931–936, 2002-05-07Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the bounded conclusions reported in the authors’ public abstract are retained; this guide did not independently review full methods and data, recertify two-way channel effects or historical increments from the abstract, or generalize to obligations in human relationships.

What it limitsShared input can explain correlation, while mutual benefit is an additional value/outcome judgment.

What does not follow

  • If only one direction is identifiable, retain its one-way effect without filling in the other.
  • A shared environment or common measurement timing can produce synchrony; report cadence is not object coupling.
  • A terminal-value summary sufficient for one task is not automatically usable for deadlines, peaks, or targeted intervention.
  • A relationship’s ability to persist creates no obligation to maintain it; two-way effects can also amplify harm.
  • This guide cites only conclusions reported in the original authors’ public abstract for the real case; methods and individual data were not independently reviewed here, and nothing is certified as a formal test.

Scope and open questions

The original abstract provides an explicit example of antagonistic two-way adaptation. Reading scope and support ceilings are disclosed; the mathematical model explains only nonequivalence despite a shared terminal state and does not masquerade as biological data.

  • Independent evaluation of the biological experiment's channel identification, temporal resolution, and competing explanations would require obtaining and checking the full methods and data. This lesson does not fill those gaps from the abstract.

Why do two models converging to 0 differ on meeting a second-step threshold?

Maximum row sums bound convergence rates; the particular two-step differences follow from matrix recurrence. From the given initial state, A’s second-step maximum is 0.125 and B’s 0.578125, giving different results against threshold 0.2.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If only current y increases by one unit, how much does next-step x change in each model?

A increases by 0.25 and B by 0.125; sharing a fixed point does not guarantee the same intervention response.

If A affects B and B also changes, is that enough for two-way coevolution?

No. Independently trace B→A’s actual effect, timing, and comparison; B’s change cannot replace a return-direction mechanism.

If both directions have persistent carriers, must both sides run a historical-increment test?

No. Carrier routes require separate evidence; only each additional historical-increment claim additionally requires a historical-increment test.

Can coevolution be asymmetric and antagonistic?

Yes. Two-way influence is neither symmetry nor mutual benefit and creates no obligation to continue.

6.10Dissolution, Object Conversion, and the Limits of Repair ​

In briefRepair need not restore every old component, and dissolution need not mean failure. First specify what is to be preserved or regained, then compare which new states achieve that target and who has authority to choose.

The criterion for dissolution is that the original identity criterion no longer holds. If the original identity criterion fails but another object’s definition can hold, object conversion should be distinguished from termination. A phase change is distinguished from dissolution only if the original identity criterion continues to hold. Dissolution does not automatically count as failure, and persistence does not automatically count as success.

The criterion for repair is a target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public before the results are seen (§3.2). Repair can make use of old traces, and it can change components, boundaries, relations, interfaces, carriers, and scale positions. It does not turn back time to an earlier state. A claim that a repair window exists requires, besides the target identity criterion or target functional criterion, a comparison of how intervening at different times affects whether the target can be reached and at what cost. Use the carrier route to obtain evidence about current constraints formed through history (§4.5). A historical-increment test is additionally required only for a claim of a historical conditional residual beyond the current representation. Even if these empirical conditions all hold, whether the goal is justified, who chooses it, who is responsible, and who may implement it must still be reviewed under the normative premises (§14.3), the scope of authorization, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6).

6.10Note

Understanding this section

6.10 Dissolution, object conversion, and repair boundaries

Repair need not restore every old component, and dissolution need not mean failure. First specify what is to be preserved or regained, then compare which new states achieve that target and who has authority to choose.

Dissolution is judged by failure of the original identity criterion. The identity criterion is only one item in the definition of the object, not the entire definition; unchanged wording does not guarantee that the object still meets it. If the original identity criterion fails while the definition of another object may hold, distinguish termination, conversion, and reclassification. Continued use of an old name does not establish continued existence of the original object.

The distinction between phase change and dissolution is whether the original identity criterion still holds. The same object may change operating regime, but when its original identity fails, that change cannot silently be called a “new phase.” A new candidate definition also cannot certify actual object conversion merely by definition. Formal conversion claims require corresponding scale mapping, preservation/loss, material from a scale-closure test (§4.6), and related conditions.

Dissolution does not automatically mean failure, nor continued existence success. Success requires prior objectives, costs, and evaluation criteria. Orderly termination may be a permitted objective, while preserving an old identity may continue harming functions or others. What remains and what has ended must be answered separately from whether preservation is worthwhile.

Repair is judged against a target identity criterion or target functional criterion disclosed before results. It may use old traces or replace components, boundaries, relations, interfaces, carriers, or scale positions. A new state meeting the target need not exactly reproduce the past. Conversely, restored appearance, an old name, or recovery of one output does not alone ensure that the predetermined target identity criterion and target functional criterion are met. If only the target functional criterion was selected, report only that functional achievement without additionally proving original object identity.

“An available repair window” is a more specific empirical claim. Beyond the target, compare how intervention timing affects reachability and cost, specifying permitted measures, resources, delays, and alternative paths. A plan becoming infeasible after some time does not imply every possible plan is permanently hopeless. New resources or technologies change the feasible set and must be disclosed, not used to rewrite the original window conclusion.

Historically formed damage, connections, or capabilities may act as current constraints; trace their formation and present effects through the carrier route. Whether history adds usefulness conditional on complete current constraints is a separate question, and only that question adds a historical-increment test. Historically caused current damage does not require every repair comparison to prove an additional historical increment.

Empirical reachability confers no implementation authority. Target justification and who chooses, bears responsibility, or may execute require review under the normative premises (§14.3), the scope of authorization, and the four-step operational procedure (§14.6): fix description and evidence; disclose normative premises and conflicts; compare options including inaction and check authorization; then bound execution, monitoring, stopping, appeal, restoration, and remedies. Technical comparisons for deliberation may be completed first without masquerading as authorized actual disposition.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check the original definition of the object and its identity criterion, specifying which states still satisfy it and when satisfaction ends.

  2. 2

    If the identity criterion continues to hold, examine phase. If it fails, separately examine termination, conversion, or reclassification; formal conversion additionally requires checks of the definition and evidence.

  3. 3

    Disclose the target identity criterion or target functional criterion before results, listing changeable components/boundaries/relations and task conditions that must not be lost.

  4. 4

    Test candidate repaired states against each target rather than requiring every old state to return or judging appearance alone.

  5. 5

    A repair-window claim requires comparison of intervention times, permitted measures, reachability, and costs, with the feasible set explicit.

  6. 6

    Separate current historical carriers from additional historical increments. Action selection additionally passes review under the normative premises, the scope of authorization, and the four-step operational procedure.

Distinctions to keep clear

Original identity criterion fails

The original identity criterion no longer permits claiming preservation of the original object.

≠

All functions disappear

A stronger claim that need not hold; other objects or functions may remain.

Repair of target identity or function

Achieving a previously declared identity or functional target.

≠

Returning to the historical original

Unnecessary; paths, components, or support may change.

Repair is reachable

The target can be achieved with specified measures, resources, and timing.

≠

Implementation is authorized

Additionally requires normative premises, authority, and bounded procedures.

One plan's window closes

The target is unreachable within the stated feasible set.

≠

Every future plan is impossible

Does not follow by extrapolation from the former.

Mathematical construction: replacing one edge can repair a functionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsGraph structure, capacities, and targets are artificial. Inputs/outputs share units and windows, capacities are realizable, and there are no additional losses. The target identity criterion is only this construction's declared criterion; complete actual objects require further material.

A fictional undirected service network has nodes a,b,c and original edges a—b and b—c, each capacity 4. The task's target functional criterion is delivery of 4 units of the same quantity type per period from a to c; the target identity criterion is connectivity among these three specified nodes. Only a supplies and c receives, b conserves flow, and there is no additional flow. The original sole path a—b—c carries 4. If b—c breaks, c is isolated, the target identity criterion is not met, and delivery is 0. A repair adds capacity-4 edge a—c while retaining a—b, reconnecting all three and directly carrying 4. The new edge set differs from the original while satisfying the target identity criterion and target functional criterion predetermined here.

BoundaryMathematical reachability certifies neither actual networks, deployment authority, nor costs. If the original identity criterion required preserving every old edge, the conclusion would differ; this must be specified beforehand.

Mathematical construction: timing changes reachability, not historical inevitabilityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDamage formation, measure range, and cost rule are explicit. There is no additional recovery while waiting or new measure, and t≥0.

Let fictional damage z_t=t for integer times starting at 0. The sole permitted measure removes m damage units once, with 0≤m≤2. After treatment z*=max(0,z_t−m), costing m budget units under budget cap 2. The target functional criterion is z*=0. At t=1, m=1 achieves it at cost 1; at t=2, m=2 achieves it at cost 2. At t=3, every permitted m leaves at least 1, so the target is unreachable. The window under these measures/budget is therefore t≤2, not impossibility of every future repair.

BoundaryOnly a target-reachability calculation, not a diagnosis of irreversible human conditions. New resources/measures require a newly declared question.

Teaching construction: renaming cannot erase affected positionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPure teaching regrouping; no boundaries of actual organizations or populations are adjusted.

Using the disconnected network, defining only a and b as a new two-point service object permits study of that new candidate, but does not restore the original service target for c. Disclose how the new definition handles c, original obligations, and exit losses. Establishing a smaller object does not automatically replace the original object's task.

BoundaryA new object's empirical validity, conversion eligibility, and normative adoption require separate evidence, not renaming.

Temporary island microgrids: functional repair need not restore the original connection exactlyDocumented case

GAO's 2019 report records that Vieques and Culebra previously received power through submarine transmission lines connected to Puerto Rico's main grid. As of December 11, 2018, 7 USACE-supported generators served the islands' microgrids. This section adds the observation that supply carriers/connections may differ from the originals: “the original connection was not restored exactly” and “no functional repair occurred” are not the same claim.

Scope and limitsDescribes only the replacement supply configuration in the report. It does not independently establish continuous supply to every user, preservation of the original grid's identity, or long-term net benefits, nor authorize actual modification.

What does not follow

  • Dissolution, conversion, and failure are not synonyms; continued existence likewise guarantees neither function nor value.
  • The target criteria cannot be changed after results to match what was achieved and rescue the original repair task.
  • Changing a carrier can truly repair a function. Whether the original identity criterion is preserved is checked separately; both need not always hold.
  • Repair windows are bound to object, target, measures, and resources, not unconditional permanent verdicts of fate.
  • Technical feasibility creates neither named responsibility nor authority; analytical comparison is not actual deployment.

Scope and open questions

An actual replacement supply configuration illustrates the distinction between new carriers and old configurations. Repair targets, network flows, and windows are separately explicit constructions; no original definition of the object is presumed for the disaster area.

Retaining a—b and adding a—c connects b to c through a. Edge a—c has capacity 4 and this is the only same-type flow demand, so the target functional criterion is reachable.

6.10.1Formation, Maintenance, Recovery, and Replication ​

In briefInitial formation, continued maintenance, recovery after damage, and replication elsewhere may depend on different conditions.

That an arrangement forms, that it can then be maintained, that it can recover after a disturbance, and that it can be replicated elsewhere are four outcomes, each with its own conditions and evidence. Formation usually requires start-up conditions and a path of transition from the original state. Whether maintenance depends on continuing replenishment, replacement, and correction is tested under §6.5. Recovery depends on the carriers and margins still available after the disturbance, the external replenishment that can be reached, and the time remaining; whether what recovers is output, identity or function, or internal margins is specified separately under §6.6. Aiming at a target identity criterion or target functional criterion made public in advance rather than seeking a return to the original state is called repair and is judged under §6.10. When the arrangement is replicated in a new location, the results in the original location provide only a candidate; the new location must itself have the corresponding personnel, equipment, time, and conditions for error correction, and must have its own materials.

The four are judged separately, and none can vouch for another. All four are also descriptive judgments and do not mean that the arrangement should be maintained, recovered, or replicated. Operating well in the current period can coexist with no one taking it up in the next round; that longer-term or wider-scope results have not yet been demonstrated also does not cancel local results already achieved under criteria fixed in advance. When replication or scaling up fails, distinguish at least four situations: the scheme itself fails, including cases where the results in the original location were not caused by the scheme; the scheme was not implemented as written in advance; the new location lacks enabling conditions the mechanism requires; or scaling up itself changed the treatment or the object (§2.4.1). Both what was implemented and the enabling conditions must be written down before the results are seen and be verifiable independently of the results. An implementation deviation or a missing condition raised only after failure can only be recorded as a candidate to be tested in the next round and does not change the present record.

6.10.1Note

Understanding this section

6.10.1 Formation, Maintenance, Recovery, and Replication

Initial formation, continued maintenance, recovery after damage, and replication elsewhere may depend on different conditions.

Formation asks how an arrangement arises; maintenance asks what keeps it operating; recovery asks how specified functional or identity goals are met again after damage; replication asks whether corresponding outcomes can be obtained with a different object, place, or scale. These four can have different answers, and earlier success guarantees no later stage.

Recovery here connects to repair among the basic state terms (§3.2): specify the functional or identity goal, without automatically interpreting recovery as a return to the historical original. Maintenance may rely on different people, resources, and rules from formation. Replication may face different capabilities, authority, external conditions, and scale effects.

Failure of replication or expansion requires comparing at least four possibilities: the scheme itself failed, including that it did not cause the original result; implementation departed from the content specified beforehand; the target lacked enabling conditions specified beforehand; or scale changed the treatment or object. Each explanation needs independently checkable evidence, not selection after failure to protect the original conclusion.

Implementation content and enabling conditions must be stated before outcomes and independently checkable. ‘The conditions were actually wrong,’ introduced only after failure, enters only as a candidate for the next round. Records obtained after outcomes that check previously declared conditions should be evaluated as evidence, not categorically excluded merely because collection was late.

Terms used here

Formation and maintenance
Conditions for emergence and for continued operation require separate evidence.
Replication conditions
Implementation content and enabling conditions declared before outcomes and independently checkable.

From the source

The four are judged separately, and none can vouch for another. All four are also descriptive judgments and do not mean that the arrangement should be maintained, recovered, or replicated.

6.11Final Gate for Mechanism Outputs ​

In briefAfter writing a mechanism explanation, ask again: what evidence have we actually delivered, and how far may the conclusion go? This overall gate prevents “the system has feedback” from quietly becoming “the system has learned, recovered, and deserves preservation.”

For each of the six conditional mechanisms, the following must be set out clearly, in this order: the statement of object and scale, inferential premises, enabling conditions, mechanism chain, minimum evidence, competing explanations, counterexamples, and failure boundary. If any item is missing, retain only a candidate mechanism or a question to check. A determination of feedback does not carry with it a determination of learning. Likewise, instantaneous load does not carry accumulation with it, a basic phase does not carry hysteresis, a selection pattern does not carry a specific mechanism or a value, and maintenance and repair do not carry a duty to persist. Conceptual explanations and teaching examples only illustrate how to use these conditions. They supply no external empirical support.

6.11Note

Understanding this section

6.11 Overall gate for mechanism outputs

After writing a mechanism explanation, ask again: what evidence have we actually delivered, and how far may the conclusion go? This overall gate prevents “the system has feedback” from quietly becoming “the system has learned, recovered, and deserves preservation.”

The six conditional mechanisms here are feedback, feedback-mediated learning, maintenance, load, phase, and selection. They share eight checks: object and scale declaration, inferential premises, enabling conditions, mechanism chain, minimum evidence, competing explanations, counterexamples, and failure boundaries. A common framework does not mean the same evidence for every mechanism or a historical-increment test for every branch.

Object and scale declarations specify who is discussed and within which scope of scale, time window, and identity criterion. Inferential premises state what the conclusion logically relies on; enabling conditions state what the process needs; the mechanism chain connects actual sites of effect. Minimum evidence specifies supporting material; competing explanations check alternatives that could change judgment; counterexamples specify conditions limiting or refuting the claim; failure boundaries state when extrapolation stops or the definition changes.

The eight items cannot substitute for one another. Drawing a chain does not supply evidence; listing competing explanations does not exclude them; stating a time window does not establish observational coverage; filling in every item does not guarantee semantically correct variables, channels, or authorization references. The overall gate requires substantive proportionality, not certification merely because a table has no blanks.

Each mechanism retains its own conclusion ceiling. Feedback establishes an effective return without cross-round learning. Immediate load concerns a same-window gap without accumulated damage. Basic phase patterns do not include historical-increment hysteresis. Selection patterns do not include specified carrier mechanisms, still less value superiority. Maintenance and repair do not create perpetual preservation duties. Further claims may be proposed, but require the material they actually need.

Missing items leave candidate mechanisms or specific questions to check; broad narratives cannot fill blanks. What pauses is the determination of the complete mechanism at the claimed level, not independently established observations, domain conclusions, or lower-level results. If parameters demonstrably changed but evidence of use is insufficient, for example, retain the update fact and mark carrier-mediated learning insufficiently identified.

Also distinguish “explicit counterevidence” from “material not yet available.” Proof that a necessary condition fails blocks that particular mechanism route. An undetermined necessary condition remains unresolved rather than establishing that the mechanism does not exist in the world. Null conclusions require their own comparisons, sensitivity, and tolerance; failure of positive support is no substitute.

Conceptual explanations and teaching constructions show how these conditions are used. Exact reproducibility within a construction does not mean an external object follows its rules. Adding one real fact does not automatically empirically validate an entire model. The overall gate helps readers locate gaps without claiming actual reader testing or automatic replacement of domain judgment.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify which of the six mechanisms, which branch, and which conclusion level is at issue, avoiding interchangeable names.

  2. 2

    Check all eight common responsibilities individually, connecting each to material for this object and window.

  3. 3

    Explicitly add conditions where stronger claims require them; do not impose a historical-increment test or governance permissions indiscriminately on every route.

  4. 4

    Distinguish a written explanation, proportionate material, completed testing, and the result obtained.

  5. 5

    When items are missing, identify specific candidates/questions and stopping points, preserving independently known facts.

  6. 6

    Record counterevidence and unknowns separately; retain distinct statuses for concepts, formal constructions, and actual empirical support.

Distinctions to keep clear

Complete explanation

Readable text addresses all eight responsibilities.

≠

Substantive support

Each item has proportionate material and actual tests; existence of text does not establish this.

Candidate mechanism

An explanation worth further examination according to its specific gaps.

≠

A supported mechanism

Meets the corresponding scope and branch conditions, permitting a bounded conclusion.

A higher-level claim remains unproved

For example, a learning-mechanism chain still lacks evidence of actual use.

≠

Lower-level facts denied

For example, the parameter change itself may already be confirmed and does not disappear.

Missing evidence

A necessary condition cannot yet be confirmed.

≠

Counterevidence

Proportionate material refutes a condition or claim; closure differs.

Teaching construction: locating gaps in a “learning report”Teaching scenario

AssumptionsA fictional arrangement of material, unrelated to an actual organization. Arrival/change/storage are checked by assumption; use is considered in two cases, unknown and known not to hold.

A fictional report accurately records feedback arrival, parameter change, and storage of the parameter file, but contains no material showing that later tasks read that version. The overall gate should neither declare “nothing happened” nor announce completed learning: update facts can be preserved, with gaps in actual use and task differences explicitly listed. If additional material shows that the program always reads the old version, this is more than missing evidence: the use claim has counterevidence.

BoundaryThis construction is not a diagnosis of actual learning and does not replace evidence collection in real domains.

Mathematical construction: text in all eight items does not mean eight resolved requirementsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBinary markers demonstrate logical non-implication. Reality also requires multiple states such as unresolved; 0 cannot uniformly be read as empirical counterevidence.

Let c_i=1 mean item i contains text, and e_i=1 mean its substantive condition has proportionate support. A model record may have (c₁,…,c₈)=(1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1) while (e₁,…,e₈)=(1,1,1,1,0,0,1,1): minimum evidence and competing explanations remain unresolved. Thus ∏c_i=1 while ∏e_i=0; formal completeness cannot replace substantive completeness. Here e_i is only a teaching logic marker; actual support cannot be created by the author entering a 1.

BoundaryThis product is not a recommended automatic fact-certification algorithm; it is only a counterexample.

Teaching construction: blocking smuggled-in conclusions individuallyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsComposed entirely of constructed inferential leaps, not descriptions of actual people or events.

Six fictional statements: return changes a state once → permanent learning; one hour's demand exceeds capacity → cumulative damage must exist; two threshold ranges → additional history must exist; differential-retention pattern → a particular inheritance channel is proved; a device needs maintenance → someone has a permanent obligation; functional repair is feasible → an institution may implement it immediately. Every arrow lacks different bridging material; “complete system mechanism” cannot supply them all.

BoundaryThis illustrates gap identification only, without prejudging all conclusions as necessarily false once material is supplied.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleEight headings are complete and the JSON passes, so all six mechanism classes hold in reality.

What it limitsSyntactic completeness generates no object facts, causal support, or normative authorization.

Teaching counterexampleThe learning route lacks use material, so the earlier parameter-change record must also be false.

What it limitsMissing higher-level evidence cannot erase lower-level known facts.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleA claim has not yet been tested, so a null mechanism is recorded as supported.

What it limitsNot tested, unresolved, and null conclusions must remain distinct.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The overall gate is a set of substantive responsibilities, not a counter of how many items are filled in or a ninth cause in the physical process.
  • The eight items unfold in logical order; new counterexamples may require revisiting premises. One linear completion does not promise permanent validity.
  • Failure of one branch does not automatically establish another; each requires its own prior claim and material.
  • Teaching examples generate no external empirical support, and passing machine validation certifies neither facts nor norms.
  • Missing items do not erase independently established facts, but prevent combining those facts into a complete claim that remains unsupported.

Scope and open questions

This section concludes the six mechanisms' common output responsibilities, suitably illustrated by logical counterexamples and explicit teaching scenarios; no historical fact is forced into service as a shared certification of every mechanism.

6.12Operation with Multiple Asynchronous Clocks ​

In briefA sentence can be heard within seconds, relational expectations may change only after several interactions, and organizational resources and institutional execution have their own cycles. Stamping all changes with the same date both misjudges delayed effects and inflates temporary responses into lasting achievements.

A multi-circle joint state includes at least five clocks: immediate, interactive, organizational, institutional, and long-term (§10.7). An event can first change fast variables, then change expectations about relationships through repeated interaction, then change resources through organizational decisions, and only then potentially lead to institutional write-back. If these changes are compressed into one moment, a delay can be misread as a lack of effect, or a short-term fluctuation as long-term evolution.

Changes in fast variables do not automatically indicate long-term institutional outcomes or outcomes in everyday life. Industrial expansion, a signed agreement, the end of overt violence, the completion of facilities, or public cooperation still calls for checking execution, distribution, rights, relations, and continuity. If the material is insufficient, retain the local results that are known and stop extrapolating over longer ranges.

Each mechanism should state which clock it updates on and what its bridges across clocks are. The arrival of a feedback signal does not establish that organizational rules have changed. An organizational decision does not amount to institutional execution. A change in institutional text does not imply actual write-back at every local position. A bridge across clocks must specify the carrier, execution, confirmation, and failure conditions.

Clock TransitionMinimum Evidence for the BridgeCommon Failures
Immediate→InteractionA difference in state persists over multiple rounds and changes the other party’s responseA one-off emotional reaction fades
Interaction→OrganizationChanges in relations or strategies are incorporated into roles, processes, resources, or recordsVerbal consensus is not put into practice
Organization→InstitutionVerifiable changes in rules or procedures, arrangements for responsibility, and actual execution. Authorization, legal validity, and normative justification are stated separatelyA document is issued without implementation, or an institutional change that actually occurred is omitted because it lacked legal validity
Institution→Long TermContinued execution, maintenance, learning, and alternative pathsRebound after short-term compliance

The table records how changes actually follow one another step by step. Legal validity, normative justification, and authorization do not serve as criteria for establishing that “an event occurred.” Rule changes and their execution must enter the process record if there is corresponding factual evidence, even when they violate rules, exceed authorization, or are contested. Their authorization and legal status are noted separately. Explaining how they formed and what consequences they had does not amount to permitting their implementation. Conversely, authorization, issuance of a rule, or an institution’s announcement of completion cannot substitute for evidence of actual execution.

6.12Note

Understanding this section

6.12 Operation Across Asynchronous Multiple Clocks

A sentence can be heard within seconds, relational expectations may change only after several interactions, and organizational resources and institutional execution have their own cycles. Stamping all changes with the same date both misjudges delayed effects and inflates temporary responses into lasting achievements.

A multi-circle joint state distinguishes at least five clocks: immediate, interactional, organizational, institutional, and long-term. A clock here specifies when a class of variables updates and within what window it is observed, not a fixed universal duration for each event type. One event may first change fast variables, then affect relational expectations through repeated interaction, then change resources through organizational decisions, and finally possibly enter institutional write-back. “May” does not mean that every step necessarily occurs.

The minimum immediate→interactional bridge requires a state difference to persist across multiple rounds and alter the other party's response. A single fading emotion cannot count as a stable interaction rule; equally, before the next round arrives, ineffectiveness cannot be declared prematurely. Record what carrier retains the state, whether subsequent contact occurs, and the other party's actual response.

Interactional→organizational transition requires relational or strategic changes to enter roles, processes, resources, or records. Verbal agreement and a meeting's atmosphere cannot replace implementation; role adjustments, scheduling, budgets, and work-record versions and execution each have their place. A judgment of organizational change still cannot leap directly to all institutional constraints having changed.

The organizational→institutional bridge requires verifiable changes in rules or procedures, arrangements for responsibility, and actual execution. Authorization, legal validity, and normative justification are listed separately. Publishing a document cannot replace execution; unauthorized or disputed conduct also cannot justify omitting institutional effects that actually occurred. Recording facts is neither endorsement nor permission to implement them again.

Institutional→long-term transition requires tracing continuing execution, maintenance, learning, and alternative routes, including checking for rebound after short-term compliance. Long-term is not a label stamped in advance: coverage periods, seasons, demand fluctuations, membership changes, and continuity of support must fit the claimed outcome. If observation ends on a particular date, persistence after that date cannot be fabricated.

Every cross-clock bridge specifies its carrier, execution, confirmation, and failure conditions. The carrier may be parameters, records, schedules, rules, or other states, but must be located. Execution specifies how an update actually enters a process; confirmation specifies where change is independently checked; failure conditions specify when the bridge fails to connect. Reposts sharing one publication source do not automatically add independent confirmation of execution.

Relatively fast results such as industrial expansion, signed agreements, cessation of public violence, completed facilities, and public cooperation may all have real value, yet cannot settle long-term living conditions. Continue checking execution, distribution, rights, relations, and persistence. When material is insufficient, preserve locally known results and stop distant extrapolation, neither canceling local achievements nor inventing final success.

Factual clocks and normative states cannot be merged. If rule changes or execution actually occurred, record them in the process timeline with their corresponding status, even if they violated rules, exceeded authority, or were disputed. Conversely, authorization, publication of an announcement, or an institution's declaration of completion does not mean actual execution at every local position. Both confusions distort causal timelines.

Thus distinguish no short-term change from delayed effects not yet reaching the observation window, and short-term fluctuation from long-term evolution. Update times and observation times may differ; missing records do not automatically mean absent events. But a promise of future effects cannot replace evidence missing now. Report according to each claim's horizon and stop where bridges remain unverified.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Declare update clocks and observational coverage separately for immediate, interactional, organizational, institutional, and long-term variables.

  2. 2

    For immediate-to-interactional transition, check repeated rounds, state retention, and the other party's response; a single emotion cannot replace them.

  3. 3

    For interactional-to-organizational transition, check actual entry into roles/processes/resources/records; for organizational-to-institutional transition, check rules, responsibility, and execution.

  4. 4

    For institutional-to-long-term transition, check continuing execution, maintenance, learning, and alternative routes, preserving rebounds and uncovered periods.

  5. 5

    For each bridge, locate carriers, execution, confirmation, and failure conditions, distinguishing event time, record time, and publication time.

  6. 6

    State factual records alongside authorization, legal validity, and justification; neither erase events through illegality nor manufacture execution through approval.

  7. 7

    Preserve locally known achievements; stop extrapolation beyond the horizon or population and to ultimate effects on living conditions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Event time

When an action or state actually changes.

≠

Announcement / record time

May precede or follow execution and is not interchangeable with it.

Rule publication

A text or decision appears.

≠

Actual institutional execution

The process by which a rule enters specific positions, requiring independent material.

Authorization / justification status

Judgments concerning norms and permissions.

≠

Whether it actually occurred

An empirical-record question; the two cannot replace one another.

Bounded short-term achievement

Evidenced within a particular window, object, or function.

≠

Comprehensive long-term outcome

Requires continued checking of persistence, distribution, rights, and relations.

Teaching construction: compressing several dates into one produces errorsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDates, events, and coverage are teaching assumptions. Every bridge is given in the example's text; no actual institution is claimed to operate this way.

A fictional system receives feedback on day 0. Two interactions on days 1 and 3 show that the update persists and changes the other party's response. The organization decides on day 5, resources are actually allocated on day 6, a new procedure is published on day 8, and actual execution begins on day 10. If the task requires institutional execution by day 9, this construction fails; the day-8 announcement cannot substitute. If the question is only whether execution had occurred by day 11, one may answer that it had begun. The long-term target runs to day 90, but material covers only day 30, leaving 60 days unobserved. Beginning execution on day 10 is not sustained success through day 90.

BoundaryMeeting a deadline, beginning execution, and sustained attainment differ; lateness relative to day 9 is not permanent ineffectiveness.

Mathematical construction: factual and authorization bits do not imply one anotherTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExplicitly given binary teaching records, not a determination of any actual conduct's legal status.

Let E=1 mean an action was actually executed and J=1 mean the construction's prespecified permission conditions were satisfied. Case A, (E,J)=(1,0): the action occurred but permission conditions failed; both the fact and the excess-of-authority status must be recorded, without changing E to 0. Case B, (E,J)=(0,1): authorization exists but execution has not occurred, so E cannot become 1. Discussion of legal validity or normative justification requires separate items; one J bit cannot handle them all.

Boundary“It happened” cannot imply “it may continue to happen,” nor can authorization establish actual achievements.

Teaching construction: an unexperienced season does not cancel current attainmentTeaching scenario

AssumptionsNo actual facility or performance data; loads and windows are teaching conditions.

A fictional facility meets prespecified service-quality targets for one month under ordinary load, with complete records; the next season's peak has not yet arrived. Its function for this month and load range may be confirmed, but year-round peak stability cannot be declared. Conversely, an unverified peak does not turn verified ordinary-period service into zero achievement.

BoundaryPeak evaluation must be safe, feasible, and authorized; the construction does not demand forced stress testing or withdrawal of support.

Maryland renewals: submission, actual use, and approval have different datesDocumented case

Maryland's 2024 report separately records submission of the mitigation plan to CMS on September 13, 2023, use of the updated renewal process beginning in November 2023, and approval of the plan in February 2024. This section adds the observation that these three event types do not share one date; implementation, plan approval, and long-term results require separate evidence. Temporal order alone cannot determine the legal status of every action at the time, and the report does not use this timeline to establish long-term health effects.

What does not follow

  • The five clocks impose neither a universal sequence nor fixed numbers of days; actual processes may interleave, return, or stall.
  • Every cross-clock bridge can fail. Success at an earlier level does not guarantee the next, and aggregate labels cannot bypass them.
  • Illegality, excess of authority, or dispute does not turn actual effects into non-events; explaining their formation grants no permission to implement them.
  • Approval and plans cannot replace execution; temporary non-observation of later effects also cannot justify declaring permanent ineffectiveness without a window.
  • When long-term material is not yet available, retain unknowns; do not forcibly withdraw necessary support or create dangerous interruptions for verification.

Scope and open questions

The same official report separates submission, use, and plan approval, making it suitable for distinguishing multiple clocks. Teaching dates and the binary-authority example are separately marked fictional, avoiding legal judgments about the real case.

6.13Cross-Circle Cascades and Coevolution ​

In briefA message crossing a bridge does not mean people, resources, and action cross along with it. Cross-circle analysis must separate every hop: what exactly was transmitted, on what grounds does the next location change, and where does the process stop?

A cascade occurs when a local change in one circle[1] triggers changes in other circles through overlapping membership, bridging interfaces, shared resources, network propagation, or top-down institutional transmission. The object, channel, scale, and evidence need to be checked again at each step. The first step holding does not warrant assuming that all later steps hold. Capacity limits, filtering, delays, offsetting effects, and local exclusion zones can cut a cascade short.

A discussion of cross-circle propagation must first identify what propagates and what conditions the target needs in order to change. A message can arrive through a single bridge. An action that requires actual cooperation from several people, confirmation from different sources, or adequate support for acting safely can stall in that same network. A count of relays from one source cannot stand in for a count of independent confirmers, and a count of confirmers cannot stand in for actual collaboration. A bridge’s effect depends on how the sources are related, where the transmission arrives, the order of arrival, the duration of action, and the conditions of feasibility. It cannot be determined directly from the shortest path, the number of connections, or any one model threshold.

Three situations must also be distinguished: one failure triggers the next; multiple failures jointly obstruct recovery; or a common external cause damages multiple locations at the same time. The first requires evidence of transmission at each hop. The other two require checks on the conditions on which recovery depends and on exposure to common causes, respectively. A mechanism by which people adopt something only after confirmation from multiple sources can coexist with supply dependencies among facilities, but their state variables and thresholds cannot be interchanged. Complex contagion does not guarantee that higher clustering is more beneficial. The gains it brings from reinforcement can be offset by reduced reach across groups.

Coevolution requires at least two objects to change one another’s selection environments, transition probabilities, or constraints over a period of time while retaining their own independent identity criteria. If one object is simply absorbed by another, it should be recorded as nesting or object conversion. Synchronized changes due solely to a common external environment are not called coevolution. If a return signal changes no subsequent state, the relationship is called only coupling or shared exposure.

Multi-circle cascades and coevolution carry no inherent direction of value. Tighter coupling can improve coordination or increase vulnerability and diffuse responsibility. Decoupling can reduce efficiency or protect local autonomy and the ability to limit losses. Evaluation and action still belong to the normative layer (Part 14).

6.13Note

Understanding this section

6.13 Cross-circle cascades and coevolution

A message crossing a bridge does not mean people, resources, and action cross along with it. Cross-circle analysis must separate every hop: what exactly was transmitted, on what grounds does the next location change, and where does the process stop?

A cascade occurs when a local change in one circle triggers changes in others through channels. Channels may include overlapping membership, bridging interfaces, shared resources, network transmission, or downward institutional action. Membership overlap may let the same person take up two positions; shared resources may transmit use at one location into shortage elsewhere; downward institutional action may change local procedures. These are mechanism types requiring specific identification; their names do not establish that they have occurred.

Recheck objects, channels, scales, and evidence at each level. A change at A and support for A→B do not imply B→C, much less C's long-term outcomes. Observational units, tasks, states, windows, and identity criteria may change across circles; specify their correspondence instead of reusing the first location's effect size or threshold. Insufficient capacity, filtering, delay, cancellation, and local exclusion zones can all interrupt continuation.

First ask what spreads: message arrival, opinion confirmation, adoption, actual cooperation, receipt of funds, and equipment supply are different state variables. A message may cross a single bridge; action may require multiple participants to be available in the same window, confirmation from different sources, and safe on-site conditions. A network path establishes only possible connectivity in the model, not the feasibility of real action.

The same message arriving through three channels may still have only one original basis. Confirmation by different people also requires checking their source relationships and cannot automatically count as statistically independent samples. Even genuine confirmation from separate sources does not mean these people have actually cooperated. A bridge's endpoint determines where signals concentrate; sequence and duration determine whether conditions can be satisfied simultaneously; safety and authority have separate responsibilities.

A failure triggering another requires checking channels, alternative explanations, and effects hop by hop in temporal order. Multiple failures jointly obstructing recovery require checking which recovery resources must arrive together. A shared external cause damaging multiple locations requires checking common exposure. These three graphs may coexist in one accident, but multiple locations having problems cannot uniformly be written as serial contagion.

People's adoption through multiple sources and facilities' supply dependencies may influence one another, but using the same threshold cannot dispense with explanation. The former concerns information sources, trust, intentions, and action conditions; the latter may concern power capacity, logistical accessibility, and material specifications. ‘Needs two neighbors,’ if merely a model rule, is neither a universal law of human behavior nor a physical law of a power grid.

Clustering describes connections among local neighbors, not whole-network coverage directly. Local closure may reinforce signals while concentrating contact in groups already reached, reducing cross-group endpoints and effective multi-source access. A real experiment finding better diffusion in one kind of clustered network can coexist with limited cross-group coverage in another explicit model. Neither may be elevated into a monotonic law for all networks.

Coevolution additionally requires at least two objects to mutually change choice environments, transition probabilities, or constraints over a period, while retaining their respective independent identity criteria and corresponding object identities. The identity criterion is only one item within the complete definition of the object, not the whole definition. Synchronization from a common external cause alone, one-way influence alone, or return signals that do not alter subsequent states are insufficient for coevolution as defined here.

If the original two objects are merely merged or absorbed, first check nesting, interrupted identity, or object transformation; ‘they are now hard to distinguish’ is not the strongest proof of coevolution. Descriptive object change still differs from a formal transformation determined by a scale-closure test (§4.6), which requires its own transformation evidence. Independently supported domain observations do not become invalid for not having passed through a formal test in this framework.

Cascades and coevolution carry no inherent value direction. Tight coupling may aid coordination or amplify vulnerability and diffusion of responsibility; decoupling may sacrifice efficiency or protect autonomy and limit losses. Knowing a channel exists does not permit using it to manipulate people or intervene. Evaluation and action still require the normative level to judge targets, prices to be paid, rights, responsibilities, and authorization.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Fix the change to explain, starting point, target objects, and window, stating states and scales separately at each level.

  2. 2

    Identify whether each edge actually transmits messages, resources, behavior, or rules; specify channels and enabling conditions.

  3. 3

    Check starting-point change, arrival, target response, and competing explanations hop by hop. Retain unresolved status at bridges not yet checked; do not continue the chain automatically.

  4. 4

    For multi-source claims, check original sources, dependencies, and endpoints; for cooperation claims, check personnel, timing, duration, and feasibility conditions.

  5. 5

    Separate serial failure transmission, joint recovery dependencies, and common-cause exposure; map them together if needed, without exchanging edge meanings.

  6. 6

    Place clustering, edge counts, and shortest paths within the declared dynamic rules; model calculations prove only within-model results.

  7. 7

    When claiming coevolution, check both independent object definitions, mutual change, and the sustained window, excluding one-way effects, common external causes, and absorption.

  8. 8

    Report interruption points, local knowns, and out-of-scope unknowns; evaluation or real action requires separate normative and authorization responsibilities.

Distinctions to keep clear

Message arrival

Information has entered the target's receiving position.

≠

Action occurs

The target possesses and actually satisfies conditions for adoption, cooperation, and resources.

Repeated relaying

May originate from the same original basis.

≠

Multi-source confirmation

Requires checking origins and dependencies, and does not automatically equal actual cooperation.

Failure cascade

An earlier failure triggers a later one through a channel.

≠

Recovery dependencies

Multiple supplies jointly determine whether recovery is possible, without necessarily causing each other's initial failure.

Common external cause

The same exposure causes changes in multiple locations.

≠

Mutual change

Each object changes the other's subsequent conditions, requiring separate evidence for each.

Local clustering

A structural feature of connections among neighbors.

≠

Whole-network coverage

Also depends on seeds, bridging, dynamic rules, and action duration.

Coevolution

Object identities are retained separately, with continuing mutual change.

≠

Absorption/transformation

Original object relations or identities undergo a different kind of change; names alone cannot settle it.

Teaching construction: three relays, two confirmations, and one action windowTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe fictional rules separately define source deduplication, personnel availability, and duration. Time uses abstract units. Safety, equipment, and authorization are assumed satisfied only in the final feasibility judgment, without claiming actual occurrence. Distinct sources are not additionally assumed statistically independent.

Fictional target T receives three messages from P, Q, and R, all traceable to the same record O. If the rule requires two distinct original verification sources, the current source count is 1; three arrivals still fail the requirement. Adding source V later raises the source count to 2, but still does not satisfy a separate ‘two people cooperating simultaneously’ rule. Let the action window be [0,3), with P available only during [0,1) and Q only during [2,3). Their availability intervals have an empty intersection, so action cannot start under this rule. If Q instead is available during [0.5,1.5), the intersection is [0.5,1), only 0.5 units. A requirement of 1 continuous unit still fails; a requirement of 0.5 units is feasible if all other conditions are met.

BoundaryThis establishes only the nonequivalence of arrival, confirmation, and cooperation; two sources or 0.5 time units cannot be treated as universal real-world thresholds.

Mathematical construction: with the same six nodes and degree three, high clustering can still stop at half the networkTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThreshold 2, seed positions, synchronous updating, and permanent activation are explicit teaching assumptions. Node identities are fixed, with no outside seeds or decay. The construction can be enumerated exactly; it is not data from a human experiment.

Take nodes 0–5 in undirected simple graphs. Graph P is a triangular prism with edges 01,12,20,34,45,53 and 03,14,25. Graph B is complete bipartite with partitions {0,1,2} and {3,4,5}, every cross-partition edge and no within-partition edges. Both graphs are connected, have 9 edges, and give every node degree 3. Define a node's local clustering coefficient as the number of edges among its three neighbors divided by 3. In P, every node has exactly 1 such edge, so average clustering is 1/3; in B it is 0. Let the initial active set be A₀={0,1}, with synchronous permanent-activation rule Aₜ₊₁=Aₜ∪{v:|N(v)∩Aₜ|≥2}. In P, only node 2 activates in round one, giving A₁={0,1,2}; each node in the other triangle receives only one cross-group connection, so activation stops at 3 nodes. In B, nodes 3,4,5 each receive from 0 and 1 in round one, giving A₁={0,1,3,4,5}; in round two, node 2 has three active neighbors, bringing the final count to 6. Thus higher clustering does not guarantee greater whole-network coverage in this complex-threshold model. P's node 2 receives local reinforcement in round one, while B's node 2 activates only in round two, also showing that local early progress differs from whole-network success.

BoundaryThis refutes the unconditional rule ‘more clustering means more coverage.’ The two topologies also change cross-group endpoints, so the difference cannot be attributed to an independently controlled causal effect of the clustering coefficient alone. It also does not refute Centola's results under that study's design.

Mathematical construction: different equations for three kinds of ‘problems in multiple places’Teaching scenario

AssumptionsBinary deterministic rules serve to distinguish the logic. The serial-transmission example has no repair; the recovery example assumes the two resources are necessary and jointly sufficient; the common-cause example ignores other paths. Here r is the model's recovery-feasibility bit, not evidence that recovery was actually executed.

In the serial-transmission model, failure bit aₜ is fixed at 1, bₜ₊₁=aₜ, and cₜ₊₁=bₜ. Starting from (a₀,b₀,c₀)=(1,0,0), states become (1,1,0) and (1,1,1), with failure entering hop by hop. The recovery model uses p and q for availability of two resources and recovery-feasibility bit r=p∧q: r=0 for 00,01,10 and r=1 for 11. This does not state that p's failure causes q's failure. The common-cause model lets external shock u determine a=u and b=u: when u=1, both fail, still without a→b. All three models can have two failure bits simultaneously equal to 1, but offer different explanations.

BoundaryReal events may include all three mechanisms simultaneously; a cross-sectional state alone cannot select one. Model equations also do not themselves establish real causal direction.

Teaching construction: two-way information lines are insufficient, and so is a common shockTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn entirely fictional conditional comparison; “actually changes” is a construction assumption. Reality requires checking versions, execution, alternatives, and both identities, not substituting two drawn lines.

Two fictional independent organizations A and B each retain complete object definitions. A changes scheduling, changing B's available resource periods; B adjusts supply accordingly, actually changing A's available schedules in the next round. Only this supplies a candidate mechanism of mutual change. If B's reply is archived without entering later scheduling, there is only communication return. If both stop work because of the same external shutdown order, first examine the common cause. If B has lost independent object identity and become an internal unit of A, examine nesting or object conversion instead.

BoundaryDoes not establish real organizational coevolution or infer normative justification for any restructuring from mechanism feasibility.

The 2010 online-forum experiment: diffusion of registration behavior, not health outcomesDocumented case

Centola randomly assigned participants to clustered lattice and rewired random networks while preserving node degree. The behavior being diffused was registering for a health forum; registered neighbors each triggered invitations. The study reports wider, faster diffusion in the former. The additional point here is signals from different neighbors who have adopted and the network structure; total message-forward counts cannot replace them.

SourceCentola 2010, original paper publicly hosted by the author's institutionScience 329 (2010), methods and results on printed pp.1194–1196; limitations on pp.1196–1197 (PDF pages 2–5)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsAnonymous participants could not contact one another directly. Forum registration does not equal improved health, and the paper establishes neither a universal hard threshold nor a monotonic clustering law. The main text was checked; supplementary material and raw data were not independently verified.

Read the case and sources

Restoring power after the 2017 hurricanes: logistical supply as a condition of recoveryDocumented case

In its 2019 report, GAO identifies recovery barriers from documents and interviews: ports and airports in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands lacked power after the hurricanes, hindering delivery of repair materials; simultaneous recovery in many locations also raised material demand and strained supply. This section adds attention to continuity of recovery resources rather than repeating power-restoration percentages.

SourceU.S. Government Accountability Office, GAO, report dated 2019-04-18GAO-19-296, printed pp.18–19, ‘Logistical challenges’ and ‘Availability of materials’ (PDF pages 22–23)Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe report supports logistical and material constraints during recovery. It cannot establish that every initial failure propagated hop by hop, or justify applying human multi-source-adoption thresholds to electricity and logistics; the complete causal network has not been independently reconstructed.

GAO-19-296: 2017 Hurricane Season—Federal Support for Electricity Grid Restoration in the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico

Teaching counterexampleTwo objects change simultaneously, or have merged into one object, so coevolution is established.

What it limitsCommon external causes and identity conversion require separate checks; synchronization or merger does not imply mutual change between two objects.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • An established earlier level does not remove later levels' need for their own evidence. Failure may interrupt a chain locally; the choice is not all success or all failure.
  • The number of source people is not inherently the number of independent samples, and the number confirming is not the number present to cooperate.
  • Temporal order is one type of information required for mechanism identification; order alone does not establish a causal edge.
  • Human threshold models, facility-supply constraints, and counts of same-source messages have different semantics and cannot be reused directly by relabeling.
  • High clustering may strengthen local access or reduce cross-group coverage; both models and experiments must specify their networks, rules, and observed objects.
  • Check the identity criterion within each object's definition separately; unchanged criterion text does not mean an object still meets it or continues to exist independently.
  • Serial failure transmission, recovery dependencies, and common causes may mix; do not force every real event into just one graph type.
  • Edges with insufficient evidence remain unresolved. Failure to find transmission is not proof of no transmission, and model reachability is not observed occurrence.
  • Explanation, evaluation, and permission have separate responsibilities; efficient coupling does not automatically confer authority to implement.

Scope and open questions

An actual social-diffusion experiment and postdisaster logistics recovery illustrate behavioral entry and supply dependence respectively, with their statuses kept separate; models explain only differences in conditions.

  • Every step within specific circles still needs material on objects, channels, timing, and alternatives; no complete cascade identification or coevolution certification for a real case is supplied.
  • Centola's main text supports its bounded experimental results; this lesson did not independently obtain supplementary material or raw data, or conduct new participant or reader experiments.
  • Authorization and normative evaluation of actual decoupling, resource allocation, or organizational changes are not provided here.
