Can four people forwarding the same report directly count as four independent confirming sources?

No. First deduplicate original grounds and check source relationships. Arrival of four forwards can remain a fact; independent support cannot be accumulated by headcount.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If each of two collaborators appears for one hour, why might they still fail to complete one hour of collaboration?

If available periods do not overlap, joint duration is 0; even a half-hour overlap fails a one-hour requirement. Total presence time cannot replace simultaneous conditions.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What is the final coverage of the threshold-2 models on a triangular prism and a complete bipartite graph, and why?

3 and 6, respectively. In the former, each node of the other triangle has only one active cross-group edge, so diffusion stops. In the latter, all three opposite-side nodes receive both seeds in the first round, then activate the remaining node in the second.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does this overturn real experiments in which clustered networks spread behavior better?

No. The teaching model supplies a counterexample with different topology, seeds, and deterministic rules; the experiment retains bounded results under its own design and behavioral indicators. Neither automatically becomes a universal law.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

When multiple failures coexist, which three explanations must at least be checked?

Sequential fault triggering, multiple conditions jointly obstructing recovery, and exposure to common external causes; examine timing, resource dependence, and common-cause material. These may coexist in reality.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

A and B exchange information, but B's information never changes A's subsequent conditions. Is that enough for coevolution?

Insufficient. Communication return has not produced effective mutual change; independent object identities, persistence windows, and actual effects in both directions must also be checked.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If lower coupling reduces transmission, should decoupling automatically be adopted?

No. Lost coordination, resource costs, rights, and responsibilities must also be compared under normative and authorization conditions; mechanism effects do not replace reasons for action.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

6.14The Search Order for Mechanisms and Paths ​

In briefSearch order is an order for finding candidates, not a ranking of which is more likely true. Being found first, having complete cards, or following a common search practice cannot promote a candidate into an identified mechanism.

For a specific question, first screen for potentially applicable mechanisms according to the object, scale, time window, and requested output. Then look for paths based on observed differences in state. The state prototypes for human collectives (Part 8) apply only to objects that meet the corresponding conditions. Actors, technical systems, and natural processes must not be assigned the same set of states merely because their names are similar.

Start the search with four kinds of material. These are the object’s current state that can be confirmed, direct changes that can be confirmed after the event, channels, capacities, and clocks that can carry later changes, and mechanisms and external disturbances not yet distinguished. Use a state’s exit conditions to propose candidate paths and observed changes to propose candidate mechanisms. Then check the enabling conditions, stages of propagation, and minimum evidence item by item. The order serves only to locate candidates. Finding one earlier does not make it more likely to be true.

When using a candidate, retain competing candidates and simple baselines that can explain the same phenomenon. Return signals should be distinguished from learning. Local overload should be distinguished from temporary rises in demand, declining capacity, and common external causes. Cross-circle cascades should be distinguished from synchronized exposure. Counterexamples and exclusions specified in the full conditions of the relevant mechanism must not be omitted merely because the search has found the corresponding mechanism.

For each candidate path, state separately the conditions under which it continues to hold, the observable changes the mechanism should produce first, signals to the contrary, and the stopping point. Without evidence of enabling conditions, a candidate can still guide observations designed to distinguish the alternatives. It cannot be promoted to an identified mechanism. An early signal must not be just a scaled-down restatement of the outcome. When paths share evidence, citing it again does not add independent support.

The search order may be adjusted in light of missed cases, misclassifications, and the cost of use. Adjustments must preserve the original limits of applicability for the mechanisms and be compared with simpler search methods. Ease of search, a complete set of cards, or the use of the same order by several analysts does not establish that a real-world mechanism holds.

6.14Note

Understanding this section

6.14 Search Order for Mechanisms and Paths

Search order is an order for finding candidates, not a ranking of which is more likely true. Being found first, having complete cards, or following a common search practice cannot promote a candidate into an identified mechanism.

This section concludes the use of Part VI: §§6.2–6.10 provide conditional mechanisms and their boundaries; §6.11 is the overall gate for mechanism outputs; §§6.12 and 6.13 address multiple clocks and cross-circle relations. This section asks how to find those materials for a specific problem without exceeding their conditions.

The first paragraph specifies two steps: filter potentially applicable mechanisms by object, scale, window, and requested output, then seek paths based on observed differences in state. Defining applicability first avoids taking a phenomenon through every mechanism in search of a matching name.

The same paragraph limits state prototypes: those for human collectives apply only to objects with the corresponding conditions. Actors, technical systems, and natural processes cannot share the same state set merely because their names sound similar. This agrees with §7.5 (‘The seven state prototypes may serve only as state prototypes for human intentional collectives’) and the state prototypes in §8.3. Two constructed examples: a device being ‘newly assembled’ and a lake ‘beginning eutrophication’ cannot be assigned human-collective prototypes such as the prototype of coalescence around an anchor merely because the wording seems similar.

The second paragraph lists four types of input material: the object's currently confirmable state; confirmable direct changes after an event; channels, capacity, and clocks able to carry subsequent change; and mechanisms and external disturbances not yet distinguished. Including the last category means making room for competing explanations from the outset of the search.

Candidates have two sources: state-exit conditions suggest path candidates, while observed changes suggest mechanism candidates. Enabling conditions, propagation stages, and minimum evidence are then checked individually. The two sources answer different questions: §8.4 says a path describes ‘how a state configuration or the object’s definition changes.’ On this lesson's interpretation, a mechanism candidate concerns which process might produce the observed change; it remains a candidate until the individual checks are complete.

Order is not probability. A candidate found first is not thereby more likely to be true. The fifth paragraph allows search order to be adjusted based on omissions, misjudgments, and cost of use. These assess search performance; they do not judge which candidate is true in this case. Treating the first match as the default answer is precisely the leap this section excludes.

The third paragraph requires retaining competing candidates that explain the same phenomenon and simple baselines whenever a candidate is used. It names three distinctions: returned signals versus learning (§6.3 requires a return to produce a retainable update that actually enters subsequent tasks); local overload versus temporary demand increases, reduced capacity, and common external causes (the full conditions of the “Load, Capacity, and Recovery” mechanism in §6.6 determine what counts as local overload); and cross-circle cascades versus synchronous exposure (§6.13 distinguishes one failure triggering the next from a common external cause damaging several locations simultaneously). A search match cannot justify omitting counterexamples or exclusions required by the complete conditions of the relevant mechanism.

The fourth paragraph requires four items for each candidate path: conditions under which it continues to hold, observable changes the mechanism should produce first, contrary signals, and stopping points. Without enabling evidence, a candidate can still organize discriminating observations, but cannot become an identified mechanism. This aligns with §6.11: if any item is missing, retain only a candidate mechanism or a question to check.

An early signal cannot merely restate the outcome in a milder form. In a constructed example, if the expected outcome is markedly longer waits, ‘waiting starts to increase’ is only a mild version of that same outcome, not an early signal of local overload. Temporary demand increases and reduced capacity can also lengthen waits, so it does not distinguish those candidates. Under §12.6, an early signal is an observable change the path's mechanism should produce first. Section 1.2 likewise calls for early and contrary signals that distinguish paths when introducing analysis of specific events. If several paths share the same evidence, repeated citation does not add independent support.

The fifth paragraph permits adjusting search order based on omissions, misjudgments, and cost of use, but requires preserving the original mechanisms' applicability boundaries and comparison with simpler search methods. Convenient searching, complete cards, or several analysts using the same order do not prove a real mechanism exists. Multiple people using the same order may share the same omissions.

The strongest objection asks why prescribe an order if it does not represent probability. On this lesson's interpretation, the order serves searching with fewer omissions and errors at a manageable cost, not ranking truth. Defining applicability first avoids seeking a name for one phenomenon across every mechanism; including undistinguished mechanisms and external disturbances among the inputs preserves space for competitors. This lesson has not compared whether these features actually reduce omissions and errors. The source requires changes to preserve applicability boundaries and face comparison with simpler search methods. Section 16.24 also bars claiming superiority to alternatives without an actual comparison. Inclusion in the framework therefore cannot establish that this order is better.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Premise: mechanism conditions and applicability boundaries are distributed across Part VI, state prototypes, and the path library. A specific problem requires a procedure for finding candidates.

  2. 2

    Connection: first define applicability by object, scale, window, and output. Then start from four types of material, deriving path candidates from exit conditions and mechanism candidates from observed changes, and check enabling conditions, propagation stages, and minimum evidence individually.

  3. 3

    Conclusion: search produces candidates and arrangements for discriminating observations, not identified mechanisms.

  4. 4

    Qualification: order is not a probability ranking. Retain competitors, simple baselines, counterexamples, and exclusions. Early signals cannot be diminished versions of the outcome, and shared evidence does not accumulate.

  5. 5

    Evidential responsibility: adjustments must preserve applicability boundaries and be compared with simpler search methods. Convenience, completeness, and multiple users are not mechanism evidence.

Distinctions to keep clear

Search order

The working order for finding candidates.

≠

Ranking candidates by likelihood

The source explicitly rejects the idea that a candidate found first is more likely true.

Path candidate

Proposed from state-exit conditions, describing how a state configuration might change.

≠

Candidate mechanism

Proposed from observed changes, identifying a process that might produce them, still awaiting checks.

Candidate

Without enabling evidence, it can organize discriminating observations but cannot be promoted.

≠

Identified mechanism

Enabling conditions, propagation stages, and minimum evidence must be checked individually.

Early signal

An observable change the mechanism should produce before the outcome.

≠

A diminished version of the outcome

Merely restating the outcome more mildly cannot make it an early signal.

Citing the same evidence in several places

Still constitutes one piece of evidence.

≠

Multiple independent supports

Must come from mutually independent materials.

State prototypes for human collectives

Apply only to objects satisfying the corresponding conditions.

≠

States with similar names

Actors, technical systems, and natural processes cannot borrow prototypes merely through names.

Teaching construction: searching for candidates when waiting times increaseTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe office, rule, window, external factors, and all observables are teaching assumptions, not any real institution or event. This example omits each candidate's continuation conditions and stopping points.

Imagine a community service office where, two weeks after a new appointment rule launches, waiting times at the document-processing counter's morning appointment sessions increase markedly. Records distinguish that counter and time slot rather than using only an office-wide mean. First define applicability: the object is the reception process, not a human collective to which state prototypes apply, so the seven state prototypes are not used. The scale is one counter and one time slot, focusing on the morning document counter while recording other counters and periods as comparisons. The window spans four weeks before to four weeks after launch. The requested output is candidate mechanisms and discriminating observations, not attribution of responsibility. The four input types are queue records by counter and time, the increase in waits, staff service hours plus the appointment system and weekly roster, and undistinguished factors such as the new rule, a seasonal epidemic, and closure of a nearby office. Candidate A, local overload: under the conditions of the “Load, Capacity, and Recovery” mechanism in §6.6, measure same-type demand and available capacity at the same position and within the same window, stating them by location and distribution. The expected prior change is a gap in which same-type demand exceeds available capacity at that counter and time, before waits become markedly longer. Contrary signals include no measurable gap there, or longer waits distributed uniformly across counters and periods. Candidate B, a temporary demand increase: office-wide arrivals should rise first. Contrary signals are unchanged arrivals or arrivals increasing only after waits lengthen. Candidate C, reduced capacity: available service hours should fall first, or individual processing times should rise with arrivals unchanged. The contrary signal is neither changing. Candidate D, a common external cause: an external factor simultaneously increases arrivals and reduces staffing, aligned in time with the changes. Contrary signals are its absence or lack of temporal alignment. Simple baseline: the before-and-after difference falls within fluctuations in the same season of previous years. Do not call ‘waiting starts to increase’ Candidate A's early signal, count the same queue record as independent support for A and B, or default to A because it comes first on the search card.

BoundaryThis illustrates only search and recording structure. It identifies no true candidate and is neither a formal case of the load mechanism nor causal identification. Only part of §6.6's complete conditions is illustrated; actual use requires returning to the source.

What it limitsBeing found first does not mean greater likelihood of truth; distinguish temporary demand growth, reduced capacity, and common external causes as well.

What does not follow

  • A search match cannot justify omitting counterexamples and exclusions specified by the complete conditions of the relevant mechanism.
  • Without enabling evidence, a candidate does not become an identified mechanism.
  • Human-collective prototypes such as the seven state prototypes (§8.3) are not applied to individuals, technical systems, or natural processes.
  • A mild version of the outcome cannot serve as an early signal. Early signals are observable changes the mechanism should produce first; when listing them, also check whether they distinguish paths (§1.2, §12.6).
  • Convenient searching, complete cards, or multiple users of the same order do not prove a real mechanism. Adjustments must preserve applicability boundaries and face comparison with simpler methods.

Scope and open questions

This section specifies a working order for finding candidates. The lesson uses a teaching construction only to illustrate search and recording; it is no formal case of any mechanism and adds no figure.

  • This section requires distinguishing local overload from temporary demand growth, reduced capacity, and common external causes. Specific observational conditions belong to the “Load, Capacity, and Recovery” mechanism in §6.6; the lesson does not prescribe a uniform criterion on the author's behalf.
  • This lesson has not compared this search order with simpler search methods.

Is a candidate found earlier more likely true? On what basis may search order be adjusted?

No. The source says the order is only for finding candidates, not evidence that earlier ones are more likely true. Search order may be adjusted based on omissions, misjudgments, and cost of use, while preserving the original mechanisms' applicability boundaries and facing comparison with simpler search methods.

Basis: §6.14, second and fifth paragraphs.

Where do path candidates and mechanism candidates respectively come from?

Path candidates come from state-exit conditions; mechanism candidates come from observed changes. Both then require individual checks of enabling conditions, propagation stages, and minimum evidence.

Basis: §6.14, second paragraph.

Which four items must a candidate path specify at minimum? What can it still do without enabling evidence?

Continuation conditions, observable changes the mechanism should produce first, contrary signals, and stopping points. Without enabling evidence, it can still organize discriminating observations but cannot become an identified mechanism.

Basis: §6.14, fourth paragraph.

If the expected outcome is markedly longer waits, why is ‘waiting starts to increase’ not an early signal of local overload?

It merely restates the outcome more mildly. Temporary demand growth and reduced capacity can also lengthen waits, so it fails to distinguish competitors. Under §12.6, an early signal is an observable change the path's mechanism should produce first.

Basis: §6.14, third and fourth paragraphs; §12.6.

Can complete cards and multiple analysts using the same search order prove a mechanism? What comparison is required when adjusting the order?

No. Adjustments must preserve the original mechanisms' applicability boundaries and face comparison with simpler search methods.

Basis: §6.14, fifth paragraph.

Takeaway

Search order is only a working order for finding candidates; earlier discovery does not mean greater likelihood of truth. Retain competing candidates and simple baselines when using a candidate. Without enabling evidence, it may still organize discriminating observations, but cannot become an identified mechanism.
